en: *The Scripture on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation*, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Teacher says: "A guide is difficult to encounter, and it is likewise difficult for those who hear [the Dharma] to rejoice."
That which the great man delights in hearing, the small man loathes to hear.
Beings are pitiable and wounded, fallen upon the perilous path of old age and death;
slaves to the love of worldly folk, they dwell in fear yet remain unafraid because of their delusion.
Whether the worlds be large or small, no phenomenon possesses permanence;
nothing endures for long, appearing but momentarily like a flash of lightning.
This body is subject to old age and death, the final destination of all maladies.
A thin skin covers impurity, yet the deluded are deceived by it.
You are constantly devoured by the thief of old age, which swallows up the vigor of youth;
like a withered flower garland, you are ruined and devoid of value.
The merit of King Mūrdhaja allowed him to sit together with the Heavenly King Śakra;
his rewards and blessings were vast and manifold—where are they all today?
Among gods and humans, this king was supreme in the possession of sensual delights.
At the time of death, there is extreme suffering; by this one may awaken the mind.
All desires are pleasant at first, but in the end they all become great suffering;
they are like an enemy who is kind at first, yet brings the calamity of exterminating one's clan later on.
This body is a vessel of impurity, with nine orifices constantly discharging filth;
it is like a malignant ulcer, for which medical treatment must be discontinued.
This bony chariot has but little strength, as the sinews and veins entwine it while consciousness revolves within.
That which you consider a sublime vehicle, you endure attachment to it without shame.
It is a place where the dead gather, where bodies are cast away and fill the graves;
that which was cherished and protected while alive is entirely abandoned at death.
One should always maintain such mindfulness, observing with a single mind without distraction;
shatter the dark gloom of delusion and inversion by holding aloft the torch of clear observation.
If one abandons the four foundations of mindfulness, there is no evil that the mind will not commit.
Like an elephant gone wild without a hook, one will never follow the path of discipline.
Today one busies oneself with this task; tomorrow one undertakes that affair.
Delighting in attachment and failing to contemplate suffering, one does not realize that the thief of death has arrived.
Hurriedly occupied with one's own affairs, one is likewise unacquainted with other matters;
yet the thief of death does not wait for the right moment, and when it arrives, there is no cause for escape.
Like a thirsty deer rushing toward a spring, having already drunk and now turning back toward the water.
The hunter, devoid of compassion, does not allow [the deer] to drink but kills it;
so too is the fool: though he busies himself diligently with various affairs, when death arrives, it waits for no time—who will protect you?
The human heart aspires for wealth and honor, yet the passions of the five desires remain unsated;
even among the ranks of great kings, none can escape this affliction.
Even the sages who wield mantra-spells and arrows cannot avoid birth and death.
Trampled by the elephant of impermanence, the anthill and the leech are one with the earth.
Setting aside all other people, even the Buddhas, the Truly Enlightened Ones—
who have crossed over the stream of birth and death— even they do not abide forever.
For this reason, you should know: whatever you find dear and pleasant, you should abandon it all as soon as possible, and with a single mind seek nirvāṇa.
When you later cast off this body and die, who will testify to me?
Furthermore, there are those who encounter the Dharma-treasure, and those who do not.
After a long time, the Buddha-sun arises, shattering the great darkness of ignorance;
by emitting all manner of radiances, it reveals to humanity the path and that which is not the path.
From where have I come? From what place was I born?
Where shall I attain liberation?
Who shall clarify this doubt?
Only the Buddha, the Sage of All-Knowledge, appears in the world after a vast interval;
do not let your mind be negligent, for he alone can sever the knots of your doubt.
He does not delight in true benefit, but takes pleasure in clinging to a corrupt and evil mind;
you have grown up among sentient beings, and you should seek the true characteristics of the Dharma.
Who can know the time of death, or by which path one will go?
Like a lamp in the wind, one does not know the moment it will go out.
The Dharma of the Ultimate Way is not difficult; the Great Sage explains it by pointing to phenomena.
He speaks of wisdom and the locus of wisdom; these two do not depend on anything external.
If you are not negligent, but always practice the Way with a single mind, you will before long attain Nirvana, the supreme state of eternal bliss.
With sharp wisdom, draw near to virtuous people; devote your whole heart to honoring the Buddha and the Dharma.
Disgusted by the impurity of the body, one leaves suffering behind to attain liberation.
In quietude, one cultivates a tranquil will; sitting cross-legged amidst the forest, one restrains the mind from negligence, awakens the intellect, and realizes all conditions.
If one does not grow weary of existence within the realms, one sleeps in peace without self-awakening;
if one does not contemplate that the world is impermanent, one feels no dread toward what is fearsome.
The afflictions are deep and bottomless; the ocean of birth and death is boundless.
The boat for crossing over suffering is not yet prepared; how can one find pleasure in sleep?
Therefore, one should awaken; do not let sleep shroud the mind.
Among the four types of offerings, know the proper measure and practice contentment.
One cannot escape the great terror; one ought to apply oneself with diligent vigor.
When all suffering arrives, regret will be of no avail.
Wearing a patched robe and sitting beneath a tree, one should accept whatever food may be obtained.
Do not, for the sake of craving flavors, bring about your own ruin.
When one knows the true nature of taste, there is no difference between the beautiful and the foul;
attachment gives rise to sorrow and suffering, therefore do not create attachment.
Within the world of karmic actions, beauty and ugliness undergo constant change;
having already experienced all things, one should restrain oneself by this very fact.
If one is among the beasts, one licks grass as its sole flavor.
In hell, one swallows iron balls, burning and intensely hot as they scatter like sparks;
if one is among the hungry ghosts (preta), one vomits pus, fire, excrement, and urine;
with mucus, saliva, and all manner of impurities, these are regarded as the finest flavors.
Whether in celestial palaces, within mansions of the seven treasures;
enjoying the flavor of sudhā, the food of devas, with celestial maidens to delight the heart;
or in the noble stations of the human realm, where the seven delicacies provide every variety of flavor.
Of all that has been experienced in the past, why do you now love it again?
As you wander through the worlds, grow weary of the experiences of suffering and pleasure;
though you have not yet attained Nirvana, you should diligently seek this benefit.
When a person who studies Chan first arrives at the master’s place, the master should ask:
"Is your observance of the precepts pure?
Are you free from grave offenses or evil heterodoxy?"
If one says, "The precepts of the five aggregates are pure; there are no grave offenses, evils,
or perversions," then next teach the Dharma of the Path.
If he says, "I have broken the precepts," one should ask him again:
"What precept have you broken?
If he says, "A grave precept," [one should ask again.]
The teacher said:

"It is like a person whose ears and nose have been cut off who has no need for a mirror; you should simply return home, recite the sutras with diligence, and exhort others to perform meritorious deeds. In this way, you may plant the causes and conditions for the Way and the Dharma in future lives, while this present life is forever cast aside."
It is like a withered tree: even if one provides it with irrigation, it will not produce flowers, leaves, or fruit.
If other precepts have been violated, at that time one should instruct them to perform repentance according to the Dharma.

If [the disciple] has already become pure, and if the teacher possesses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he shall immediately teach the Dharma for entering the path according to the specific ailment;
if he has not yet attained such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he should observe their signs or inquire of them:
"Among the three poisons, which one is predominant?"
Is sensual desire more prevalent?
Is hatred more prevalent?
Or is delusion more prevalent?
What is the observation of signs? If one has many signs of lust:

they are easily slighted by others; they keep many wives and concubines; they speak much and are full of faith; their facial expression is harmonious and pleasant; their speech is easy and fluent; they have little anger or resentment, and they also have little sorrow or anxiety.

Possessing many skills and techniques, fond of hearing and possessing extensive knowledge, attached to literary verses, skilled at discourse, capable of discerning human sentiments, yet beset by many fears.

His mind dwells upon the chamber; he delights in wearing light clothing; he thirsts for female beauty; he is attached to bedding and furnishings, garments, perfumes, and flowers; his mind is often gentle and capable of compassion; he is eloquent in speech; he delights in cultivating meritorious deeds; his intention is to be reborn in heaven; and he encounters no difficulties when among the multitude.

They judge the beauty or ugliness of others, place their trust in women, and have a raging fire of desire. Their minds are prone to regret and change; they delight in adorning themselves and take pleasure in viewing colorful paintings. They are stingy with their own possessions yet covet the wealth of others; they enjoy forming friendships and do not like being alone.

Attached to their dwelling place and following worldly customs, they are alternately startled and afraid; their will is like that of a monkey. Their vision is shallow and narrow, they act without forethought, and they easily forget what they have done. They seek only to satisfy their own whims, delighting in weeping and crying.

The body is delicate and soft, unable to endure cold or hardship; it is easily obstructed and easily gratified, incapable of enduring adversity; it feels great joy at the slightest gain and great sorrow at the slightest loss, spontaneously revealing its hidden vulnerabilities.

The body is warm with a sweaty odor; the skin is thin and the hair fine; there are many wrinkles and many white hairs; one trims the nails and grooms the beard; the teeth are white and one walks with a hurried gait; one delights in clean clothing.
His studies are not focused; he delights in wandering through groves and gardens; he is full of passions and many desires, his mind fixed upon the view of permanence.

When there is a virtuous person nearby, he anticipates their needs and offers greetings; he is fond of repeating the words of others, wearing a forced smile while enduring humiliation. He understands matters quickly upon hearing them and discriminates between the good and the bad in whatever undertakings he engages in. He feels compassion for those in suffering and distress, yet he is self-important and competitive, refusing to tolerate being encroached upon. He delights in practicing charity and welcoming virtuous people; when he obtains fine food and drink, he shares it with others. He does not dwell on petty details, setting his will upon what is vast and great; however, his eyes are fixated on sensual desires, his affairs lack completion, and he possesses no long-term foresight.

He understands worldly customs and observes facial expressions; he anticipates the thoughts of others, possesses eloquent speech and wisdom, yet his friendships are not enduring. His hair is thin and sparse, and he requires little sleep. Whether sitting, reclining, walking, or standing, he never loses his dignified deportment.

Regarding all material wealth, one can quickly provide relief in times of emergency, yet soon afterwards one regrets and cherishes it; one receives the Dharma with speed, yet soon thereafter one joyfully forgets it.
One is stingy regarding one's actions, finding it difficult to change oneself, and difficult to achieve freedom from desire; thus, the transgressions committed are slight.
Such various characteristics as these are the marks of lust.

As for the marks of a person prone to anger: they are frequently troubled by anxiety and distress; they are impulsive and harboring resentment; their physical and verbal conduct is coarse and harsh; they can endure all manner of suffering; they find everything disagreeable; they are full of sorrow and have little joy; they are capable of committing great evils; they lack a heart of compassion; and they delight in quarreling and litigation.
His countenance is haggard and withered; he frowns and casts sidelong glances. He is difficult to speak with and difficult to please; he is difficult to serve and difficult to satisfy.

His mind is like a festering sore; he proclaims the faults of others. In his disquisitions on righteousness, he is stubborn and defiant, impossible to subdue, difficult to sway, hard to approach, and hard to discourage; harboring venom that is difficult to expel.

He retains what he has received and recites it without loss; he possesses great capacity and skill; his mind is free from indolence; he acts with swift efficiency; he maintains silence regarding his expectations; and his intentions are profound and difficult to fathom.

One who can repay kindness, gather a multitude, and serve others with self-discipline; one who cannot be thwarted, can bring matters to completion, and is difficult to disturb; one who has little fear or difficulty, like a lion that cannot be subdued, who never turns back and proceeds directly forward.

He recollects without forgetting, reflects with deep consideration, recites and maintains what he has learned, is able to give extensively, does not turn back from even small gains, and serves as a teacher of sharp faculties.
He dwells apart from desires and lives in solitude, possessing little lust. His mind is constantly imbued with excellence, yet he clings to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

He gazes with a stern look. His speech is truthful and his explanations of matters are clear and decisive. He has few close friends, but is firm and resolute in his undertakings; he remembers things firmly and never forgets them. He possesses great physical strength, with broad shoulders and a large chest, a wide forehead, and even hair.
The mind is firm and difficult to subdue; what is quickly acquired is difficult to forget; it can naturally abandon desire, yet delights in committing grave offenses.
Such various characteristics as these are the signs of hatred.
The characteristics of a foolish person are:

being full of doubt and regret; being indolent and lacking insight; being self-satisfied and difficult to humble; being arrogant and difficult to receive instruction; disbelieving what is trustworthy; and believing what is not trustworthy.

Lacking respect and reverence, they place their trust and allegiance everywhere; having many teachers yet being fickle and frivolous, they are shameless and impudent. In their actions they lack forethought, and instead of following instruction, they act with perverse obstinacy.

They do not discriminate between kin and friends, do not cultivate themselves, take pleasure in teachers of heterodox paths, fail to distinguish between good and evil, find it difficult to receive instruction and easy to forget it, and possess dull faculties and indolence.

They revile and slander those who practice giving; their hearts lack compassion; they destroy the bridge of the Dharma; they fail to understand matters as they arise; they glare with angry eyes and refuse to look; they possess no wisdom or skill; they harbor many desires and expectations; and they are full of doubt while lacking faith.

They harbor hatred toward virtuous people, destroy the retribution of sin and merit, fail to distinguish between wholesome words, and are unable to recognize their own faults. They do not accept instruction or admonition; they alienate themselves from kin and harbor resentment; they are ignorant of propriety and etiquette, and delight in committing verbal abuse.

Their hair, beard, and nails grow long; their teeth and robes are covered in much grime. They are driven into service by others, fearing what they should not fear, finding sorrow in what brings joy, and taking pleasure in what causes grief. They laugh where there should be weeping and weep where there should be laughter. Forced to follow behind others, they can endure bitter hardships, cannot distinguish between various flavors, find it difficult to leave desire behind, and thus commit grave sins.
Such various [afflictions] are the marks of ignorance.
If one is a person with excessive lust, they are treated by the dharma-gate of impurity;
if one is a person with excessive anger, they are treated by the dharma-gate of loving-kindness.
If there are those with much delusion, they are treated by the gateway of contemplating dependent origination;
if there are those with much discursive thought, they are treated by the gateway of mindfulness of breathing;
if there are those who are of equal proportions [in their afflictions], they are treated by the gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Various diseases such as these are treated by various Dharma-gates. Regarding the foremost Dharma-gate for treating lustful desire:

many people practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). From the feet to the hair, the body is filled with impurities: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth; thin skin and thick skin; blood, flesh, sinews, and veins; bone marrow, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, kidneys, and stomach; large intestine and small intestine; excrement, urine, nasal mucus, and saliva; sweat, tears, filth, and dust; pus, brain, fetus, gallbladder, water, membranes, fat, and the meninges—such are the various impurities within the body.
Furthermore, as for the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*):

it is the contemplation of the livid and bloated, the disintegrated and festering with flowing blood, the smeared and spreading foul pus, the partially devoured and undigested, and the scattered bones and charred remains; this is called the contemplation of impurity.
Furthermore, a person with excessive lust has seven kinds of attachment:

attachment to beautiful color, attachment to physical symmetry, attachment to deportment, attachment to voice, attachment to smoothness and softness, attachment to sentient beings, or universal attachment.
If one is attached to beautiful colors, one should practice the meditation on the bloated corpse; the same applies to impure colors such as yellow and red.
If one is attached to physical symmetry, one should practice the meditation on the swollen body and its disintegration.
If one is attached to graceful appearance, one should contemplate the meditation on a recently deceased body with blood flowing over the bones.
If one is attached to sounds, one should practice the contemplation on the throat being constricted and life being severed;
if one is attached to fine textures, one should practice the contemplation on the vision of bones and the contemplation on withered and parched sickness;
if one loves sentient beings, one should practice the six kinds of contemplations.
If one is entirely attached [to the body], one should contemplate it universally; at times, one may perform various contemplations or other distinct observations.
This is called the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Question:
"If the body is impure, like a putrid and decaying corpse, from what could attachment arise?
If one were attached to a pure body, one should likewise be attached to a putrid, decaying, and rotting body;
if one is not attached to a putrid body, one should likewise not be attached to a pure body."
Because the two bodies are equal.
If one seeks the reality of these two, neither purity nor impurity can be found; it is because the human mind is deluded and obscured by inversion that one perceives what is not pure as being pure.
If the perverted mind is shattered, one immediately attains the contemplation of the dharma of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and realizes that [the body] is impure, deceptive, and unreal.
Furthermore, regarding a corpse—which lacks heat, life, consciousness, and the sense faculties—a person who understands this clearly does not give rise to attachment;
yet, because the body possesses warmth, life, consciousness, and complete sense faculties, the mind becomes deluded and attached through perversion.
Furthermore, when the mind is attached to form, it perceives it as pure; yet when the mind of craving and attachment ceases, one immediately knows it to be impure.
If this purity were real, it should remain eternally pure; however, that is not the case.
Just as a dog eats excrement and calls it pure, whereas from a human perspective it is utterly impure, so too this body has not a single clean place within or without.

If one were to attach oneself to what is outside the body, even if one were to take up the entire body with its thin outer skin—yielding no more than a single *nāḍa* fruit—it would still be impure; how much more so the thirty-six impurities within the body?

Furthermore, when one investigates the various impurities that serve as the causes and conditions for the body, one finds it is composed of the impure semen and blood of the parents. Having already become a body, it constantly exudes impurities; even one's clothing, bedding, and mats are foul and unclean—how much more so the place where death occurs?
By this one should know that both the internal and external aspects of birth and death are impure. [This section of the sutra text extends] from here down to the beginning of the second gate.
Furthermore, there are three grades of contemplation:
those who have newly begun their practice, those who have already practiced, and those who have long practiced.

If one is a beginner in practice, they should be instructed to cultivate the perception of breaking through the skin to remove impurities; they should contemplate a skeleton, binding their attention to this contemplative practice so that external thoughts do not arise.
Should external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, they must collect the mind and cause it to return [to the object].
If one has already practiced this cultivation, one should be instructed to mentally remove the skin and flesh and contemplate the skull bone in its entirety, not allowing external thoughts to arise;
should external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, one must collect the mind and cause it to return [to the object].
If one has practiced for a long time, one should be instructed to withdraw the mind from within the body by an inch, beneath the skin and flesh, and to fix the attention on five locations:
the crown of the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, and the region of the heart.
In this way, one dwells with the mind focused on the five locations to contemplate the bones, not allowing external thoughts to arise;
when external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, one gathers the mind back, constantly mindful of the observing mind, and restrains it whenever it wanders outward.
If the mind becomes utterly exhausted, one should abide in mindfulness upon the object of focus, relinquishing external objects and maintaining internal stability.
It is like a monkey tied to a pillar that eventually comes to rest after its agitation subsides.
The object of focus is like the pillar, mindfulness is like the rope and chain, and the mind is likened to the monkey.
It is also like a wet nurse who constantly watches over an infant to prevent them from falling;
the practitioner’s observation of the mind is likewise, gradually restraining the mind to cause it to abide in its object.
If the mind abides for a long time, it accords with the dharma of dhyāna; if one attains meditative concentration, there are three signs:
the body becomes harmonious, joyful, supple, and light; the white bones emit flowing radiance like white jade; and the mind attains still abiding.
This is the contemplation of purity.
At this time, one attains the mind of the form realm; this is called the beginner’s attainment of the mind of the form realm through the dharma of meditation.

When the mind accords with the dharma of meditation, it is the dharma of the form realm. Having attained this dharma, though the body remains in the desire realm, the four great elements become extremely vast, supple, and blissful; the complexion is pure and clean, radiant and harmonious—this is called "joyful delight."
Second, within the previous contemplation of bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*) and the appearance of white bones, light shines everywhere with a pure white color.
Third, the mind abiding in a single place is called "pure contemplation" (*śubha-vipaśyanā*); because one removes the contemplation of flesh and contemplates the bone, it is named pure contemplation.
The aforementioned three characteristics are all known by oneself and are not seen by others.
Regarding the three superior grades: those who have first begun their practice have not yet resolved their minds;
those who have already practiced for three or four lifetimes have cultivated [the path].
Long-term practice refers to training for a hundred years.

Second is the dharma-gate for treating anger: if anger is particularly prevalent, one should train in the three dharma-gates of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), whether it be the stage of initial practice, already practiced, or long-term practice.
If one is a beginner practitioner, they should be taught to speak of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and affection.
How does one regard relatives and wish for them to have happiness?

When the practitioner attains various forms of physical and mental bliss—such as obtaining clothing in cold weather, coolness in hot weather, food and drink when hungry or thirsty, wealth and honor when poor and lowly, or rest when exhausted by travel—they should wish that their loved ones may likewise obtain such various joys. They should fix their mind upon loving-kindness and not allow distracting thoughts to arise.
If the mind wanders toward various conditions, one should collect it and bring it back.
If one has already practiced this cultivation, one should be instructed to extend loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to neutral persons.
How does one bestow happiness upon neutral persons?

If the practitioner attains various forms of physical and mental bliss, they should wish for others to attain them as well; they should bind the mind to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) so that no other thoughts arise, and should gather back all distracting conditions and stray thoughts to return [to that state].
If one has practiced for a long time, one should be taught to extend loving-kindness even toward those who harbor enmity and hatred.
How does one reach them and bestow happiness upon them?

When the practitioner attains various forms of physical and mental bliss, they should wish that their enemies and haters obtain it as well, so that they may attain it just like their kin. Sharing this same single-mindedness, with a heart of great purity, they regard kin and enemies as equal; extending this widely throughout the world, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to all obtain happiness, pervading the ten directions without exception or inequality.

With a pure great mind, one perceives all sentient beings of the ten directions as if seeing oneself; they appear clearly before the mind’s eye, and upon experiencing this joy, one immediately attains the Samādhi of Loving-kindness.
Question: "One may wish for those one holds dear to attain happiness; but how can one feel compassion for, and further wish for the happiness of, those who are hateful enemies? Answer:
"One should grant them happiness.
Why is this? That person possesses various other causes for excellent and pure dharmas; how could I now, on account of a single grievance, cause their goodness to perish?"
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"This person may have been my relative or friend in past lives; how can I harbor further resentment or malice because of their current anger?
I shall endure them, for this is my own beneficial gain."
Furthermore, he reflected on the practice of the Dharma: "The benevolence and virtue [of this path] are vast and inclusive, and the power of its compassion is immeasurable; this must not be lost.
He then further contemplated, saying:
"If there were no enmity or hatred, what cause would there be for the arising of patience?"
"Patience toward living beings arises from enmity, yet enmity is my own friend.

Furthermore, the retribution for anger is most severe; among all evils, there is none greater than this. When one inflicts anger upon others, its poison is difficult to restrain; though one intends to burn others, in truth it is oneself who is harmed.
He further thought to himself:

"One who wears the Dharma robes on the outside while practicing the conduct of patience within is called a śramaṇa; how could such a person allow their countenance to change and their mind to become agitated at an unpleasant sound?"

Furthermore, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) are a thicket of manifold sufferings and the target for the reception of evils. When afflictions and evils descend, by what means can they be avoided?

It is like thorns piercing the body; the thorns of suffering are immeasurable and the many enemies are too numerous to be eliminated. One must therefore protect oneself and don the leather sandals of patience.
As the Buddha said:
"To repay anger with anger, anger remains attached to one;
by not repaying anger with anger, one can destroy a great army."
To be free from anger is the way of the great man;
the small man is prone to anger, as immovable as a mountain.
Anger is a heavy poison that brings much destruction and harm.
One must not harm others; by harming oneself, one perishes.
Anger is a great darkness, such that even those with eyes cannot see;
anger is a defilement that stains the pure mind.
"Such anger and hatred must be swiftly eradicated;
for if a venomous snake remains in one's room, it will harm people if not removed.
Thus, there are various kinds of the poison of hatred that are immeasurable.
"One should practice a mind of loving-kindness to eliminate and extinguish hatred;
this is the gate of the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness.
Third, regarding the Dharma-gate for treating excessive delusion: if delusion is particularly predominant, one should study the three types of contemplative Dharma-gates:
Whether they are beginners in practice, those who have already practiced, or those who have practiced for a long time:
if they are beginners in practice, one should instruct them, saying, "Birth conditions old age and death; ignorance conditions volitional formations."
Reflecting in this way, do not allow external thoughts to arise;
should external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, restrain them and cause them to return.

If one has already practiced this cultivation, one should teach that "volitional formations (saṃskāra) are conditioned by ignorance (avidyā)," "consciousness (vijñāna) is conditioned by volitional formations," "name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is conditioned by consciousness," "the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are conditioned by name-and-form," "contact (sparśa) is conditioned by the six sense bases," "feeling (vedanā) is conditioned by contact," "craving (tṛṣṇā) is conditioned by feeling," "clinging (upādāna) is conditioned by craving," and "existence (bhava) is conditioned by clinging."
Reflecting in this manner, do not allow external thoughts to arise; if external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, restrain them and cause them to return.

If one has long practiced this cultivation, one should be taught that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*); contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*); feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*); craving conditions clinging (*upādāna*); clinging conditions existence (*bhava*); existence conditions birth (*jāti*); and birth conditions aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Reflecting in this way, one does not allow external thoughts to arise;
if external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, one gathers them back and returns them [to the object of meditation]. Question:
"The Omniscient One possesses clear knowledge (*vidyā*), while all others are characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*); how, then, can there be ignorance within this [Omniscience]?
He replied: "Ignorance is defined as the lack of knowledge regarding everything."

In this context, ignorance is able to create future existence; it takes what does not exist as existing and what exists as non-existent, abandons all that is good and grasps at all that is evil, destroys the true nature of reality, and clings to the false and illusory.
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Ignorance":
"Being unclear regarding beneficial dharmas, And ignorant of the deeds of virtue,
One creates the causes for fetters and afflictions, Like fire produced by a fire-drill."
Attached in mind to unwholesome dharmas, they cast far away wholesome dharmas;
these thieves plunder the light of sentient beings and rob them of their light in both coming and going.
They constantly entertain notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, calculating within the five aggregates.
They likewise cannot understand the Dharma of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
like blind men entering upon various perilous paths of affliction,
they accumulate karma through their defilements, and because of that karma, the stream of suffering flows on.
One takes what should not be taken, and discards what should be taken;
rushing headlong through darkness toward the non-path, one tramples upon a stump and falls to the ground.
To have eyes yet lack wisdom—the analogy is just like this.
"Because these conditions cease, wisdom shines forth like the rising sun.
Thus it was briefly explained; from ignorance up to old age and death, it is likewise.
Question: "The dependent origination within the Buddha-dharma is extremely profound; how can those who are largely ignorant perceive this dependent origination? Answer:
“There are two kinds of deluded persons:
first, those who are like oxen and sheep;
second, those deluded persons of wrong views who are shrouded in the darkness of various false views and delusions.”
The Buddha spoke this for their sake: "One should contemplate causes and conditions in order to cultivate samādhi.
Fourth, regarding the Dharma-gate for treating discursive thoughts: if discursive thoughts are particularly excessive, one should practice the Dharma-gate of the ānāpāna-samādhi.
There are three kinds of practitioners:
those who have newly begun their practice, those who have already practiced, and those who have practiced for a long time.
For one who has newly begun their practice, they should be instructed to mindfully count the inhalations and exhalations—whether long or short—from one to ten.

If one has already practiced this, one should be taught to count from one to ten, following the inhalation and exhalation, with mindfulness accompanying the breath, bringing the mind to rest in a single place.
If one has practiced for a long time, one should be taught counting, following, settling, observing, turning the observation, and purification.
Regarding the sixfold gate and sixteen stages of the *ānāpāna-samādhi*, what constitutes "counting"?
With single-minded mindfulness, one counts as the inhalation reaches its conclusion as "one," and as the exhalation reaches its conclusion as "two."
If one has not finished counting but counts what should not be counted, or if there is an error while counting from two up to nine, one must begin again from one.
It is like a calculator who takes one and one as two, two and two as four, and three and three as nine.
Question: "For what reason is it enumerated? Answer:
"Because the contemplation of impermanence is easy to attain, because it cuts off all discursive thoughts, and because one attains single-mindedness.
The arising and ceasing of the body and mind are impermanent, yet this continuity of resemblance is difficult to perceive;
the arising and ceasing of inhalation and exhalation are impermanent, and thus they are easy to know and easy to see."
Furthermore, with the mind fixed upon counting, one abandons all thoughts and discursive reflections (*vitarka-vicāra*).

As for these thoughts and discursive reflections: they are the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, the thought of harmfulness, the thought of relatives, the thought of one's country, and the thought of immortality.

Those who seek a pure mind and wish to enter the right path should first eliminate the three kinds of coarse discursive thoughts, and next eliminate the three kinds of subtle discursive thoughts. Having eliminated these six types of discursive thoughts, they shall attain all dharmas of complete purity.
It is like a person gathering gold: first they remove the coarse stones and sand, and then they remove the fine stones and sand; in this sequence, they obtain the fine gold dust.
He asked: "What constitutes the coarse illness?"
"What are the subtle ailments?
He replied: "Sensual desire, ill will, and harmful thoughts—these three are called coarse ailments; [the others] are subtle ailments."
"Relatives, country, and the perception of immortality—these three are called subtle afflictions. Once these perceptions are eliminated, one attains all pure dharmas.

He asked: "For one who has not yet attained the Path, the fetters and latent tendencies are not yet severed; since the six modes of volitional perception are powerful and give rise to mental agitation from within, how can they be removed?"

He replied: "The mind grows weary of the world; while right contemplation can suppress it, it cannot yet uproot it. Only after attaining the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) can one uproot the very foundation of the fetters and proclivities."
What is meant by right contemplation?
"To see that for one of great desire, the pursuit of desire is suffering; having obtained it, guarding it is also suffering;
losing it brings the great suffering of grief and affliction; and when the mind attains its desires, there is the suffering of never being satisfied."
Sensual desire is impermanent, empty, and a cause of anxiety and distress; since all beings share this, one should realize it and abandon it.
It is like a venomous snake entering a person's house: if it is not swiftly removed, harm will surely follow.
Unstable, unreal, and not worthy of esteem, The various desires seek only perverted pleasure;
Just as an Arhat possessing the six supernormal powers Instructs a disciple obsessed with sensual thoughts, saying:
"Your precepts are unbroken and your discipline is pure; Do not sleep in the same room as a woman."
The venomous snake of desire fills the chamber of your heart, Entwined with craving and delight, never parting.
Since you know that body and precepts must not be violated, Why does your mind dwell constantly with the fire of lust?
You are one who has left the home-life to seek the Way; For what reason do you indulge your mind in such a manner?
Your parents gave birth to you, nurtured you, and raised you; your kinsmen, with their bonds of affection, together brought you to maturity.
All weep and lament, longing for you in sorrow; how can you abandon them and disregard their thoughts?
Yet their minds constantly dwell amidst thoughts of desire, sporting with sensual objects without weariness;
always delighting in the fire of passion, they remain together, never for a moment parting from their joy and fondness.
"Thus, in various ways, one rebukes the thought of sensual desire; thus, in various ways, one correctly contemplates to eliminate the thought of sensual desire.
Question: "How does one extinguish the thought of ill will?"
He replied: "From the moment of birth from the womb, life is constantly suffering; therein, sentient beings must not harbor anger or vexation.
If one contemplates anger and vexation, compassion will extinguish them; compassion and anger or vexation are not comparable."
If you maintain compassion, hatred and affliction will cease, just as light and darkness cannot coexist;
if one upholds pure precepts yet harbors thoughts of anger, such a person destroys their own benefit of the Dharma.
Just as elephants enter the water to bathe, And then smear their bodies with mud;
So too, all beings are constantly subject to old age, sickness, and death, Enduring hundreds of thousands of various scourges and sufferings.
How can a virtuous person harbor thoughts of sentient beings, yet further increase their suffering with anger and affliction?
If one gives rise to hatred and desires to harm another, before reaching the other person, one first burns oneself;
therefore, always maintain mindfulness of practicing loving-kindness and compassion, so that anger, affliction, and evil thoughts do not arise within.
If a person constantly contemplates practicing wholesome dharmas, this mind will always cultivate what the Buddha contemplates;
therefore, one should not contemplate unwholesome things, but always contemplate wholesome dharmas with a joyful mind.
One attains happiness in this life and likewise in the next; attaining the Way and eternal bliss is Nirvana.
If the mind accumulates unwholesome thoughts, one loses one's own benefit and harms others as well.
This is called the unwholesome loss of both self and others; even the pure mind of another is likewise extinguished.
It is like a forest-dwelling practitioner who raises his hands and cries out, "Thieves have robbed me!"
"If someone asks, 'Who has robbed you?
I answer, 'I do not fear thieves of wealth; I do not accumulate riches to seek worldly profit. What thief of wealth could possibly invade me?'"
I have gathered the jewels of all dharmas that are roots of goodness, yet the thieves of discursive thought and reflection come to destroy my profit;
while one may avoid wealth-thieves by storing it in many places, there is no place to hide when the thieves who plunder goodness arrive.
"In these various ways one rebukes anger; in these various ways one correctly contemplates to eliminate the thought of anger.
He asked: "How does one eliminate the thought of vexation?"
He replied: "Sentient beings are of hundreds of thousands of kinds, constantly tormented by various ailments that arise one after another;
the thief of death lies in wait, ever desiring to kill, as they sink beneath immeasurable sufferings."
Why do good people further inflict distress upon others, slandering and plotting harm without compassion?
Before they have even injured the other, they themselves are struck by calamity.
While the anger of worldly folk may be excused, such acts are the cause of evil karma according to the laws of the world; yet they do not say of themselves, "I am practicing virtue."
A renunciant who seeks the path of purity, yet gives rise to anger and harbors a jealous mind—
releasing poisonous fire from within cool, clear clouds— one should know that such evil transgression is exceedingly deep.

An araṇya-dweller gives rise to envy; though he be an arhat possessing the knowledge of others' minds, he instructs and reprimands you, saying, "How can you be so foolish? Why do you destroy the very root of your merit through envy?"
If you seek offerings, you should gather for yourself the roots of all merit to adorn your body;
if you do not maintain the precepts, meditate, or cultivate much learning, your dyed robes are but a hollow pretense that ruins the Dharma-body.
You are in truth a beggar and a base person—how can you seek offerings to benefit your own body?
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and hundreds of thousands of sufferings—sentient beings are constantly oppressed by these afflictions;
their physical and mental tribulations are inexhaustible, so why would a virtuous person inflict further suffering upon them?
It is like pricking a festering sore with a needle, or like a prisoner whose interrogation has not yet concluded;
when suffering and calamity envelop the body and a multitude of afflictions gather, how can compassion make it even more severe?
"Such are the various ways of censuring and vexing thoughts; such are the various ways of correctly contemplating and removing vexing thoughts. He asked:
"How does one remove thoughts concerning kinsmen?"
He replied: "One should reflect in this way:
'In the cycle of birth and death within the world, one is pulled by the conditions of one's own karma; who is a relative, and who is not a relative?'"

It is only because of ignorance that one perversely gives rise to a mind of attachment, reckoning others as one's kin; those who were not kin in past lives are reckoned as kin, those who will not be kin in future lives are reckoned as kin, and those who are kin in this life were not kin in the past.
It is like birds nesting: they gather on a single tree at dusk, but at dawn they fly away, each following its own conditions.

Family and kin are just the same; born into this world, their minds are each distinct. They become close through the convergence of conditions and distant when conditions disperse; there is no fixed reality, for they associate with one another solely through the workings of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution.
It is like dry sand: when one grasps it firmly with the hand, it coheres because of that grasp; when one releases it, it scatters.

When parents raise their children, they shall receive retribution for their old age. Because the child has received their embrace and nurturance, they ought to repay them; if one accords with their wishes, one is a relative, but if one opposes their wishes, one is a thief.

There are those who are kin yet cannot benefit and instead cause harm; there are those who are not kin yet cause no harm and provide great benefit. People give rise to affection due to causes and conditions, and because of the causes and conditions of that affection, it is further severed.

It is like a painter who, having created the image of a woman, becomes attached to it himself; this case is just the same: one generates defiled attachment within oneself and becomes attached to what is external.
You had relatives in past lives; what do they do for you now in this life?

You cannot benefit those who were your relatives in the past, nor can those who were your relatives in the past benefit you. Since neither benefits the other, it is futile to dwell on whether they were relatives or not; within the world, such relationships are neither fixed nor finite.
It is as when an Arhat instructs a newly ordained disciple who is still attached to his kin, saying:
"You are just like a wicked person who vomits up food and then wishes to eat it again!"
You have already left the household life; why then do you wish to return to attachment? Is this shaving of the head and donning of dyed robes the mark of liberation?

If you are attached to your kinsmen, you will not attain liberation; you will instead be bound again by craving. The three realms are impermanent, flowing and revolving without fixed stability. Whether they are kin or non-kin, even those who are currently your kinsmen will perish after a long time. Thus, as sentient beings revolve throughout the ten directions, kinship is not fixed; none of them are truly my kin.

"When a person is about to die, they are without mind or consciousness; their gaze is fixed and does not turn, and as their breath ceases and life ends, it is as if they have fallen into a dark pit. At that time, where are their relatives and family members?"

If at the time of birth those who were not relatives in a previous life are forcibly made into relatives through association, and at the time of death they again become non-relatives—if one reflects in this way, one should not be attached to kinship.

It is like when a person’s child dies; at once, in three places, the parents weep together. They deceive the parents and wife in the heavens, they likewise deceive those among humans, and they also deceive the parents among the nāgas. By observing these various things correctly in this way, one eliminates thoughts concerning kinsmen.
Question: "How does one eliminate perceptions of the country? Answer:

"If a practitioner contemplates this land as prosperous, joyful, peaceful, and full of good people, they will constantly be pulled by the tether of 'land-awakening' and led away to places of suffering."
Awakening the mind in this way, a person of wisdom should not harbor thoughts of attachment. Why is this?
Because the various faults and transgressions of the lands burn them, and because time passes on; furthermore, there is hunger and extreme physical exhaustion, for no land is eternally secure.

Furthermore, the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death exist in no land; having departed from the bodily suffering of this place, one encounters the bodily suffering of that place—there is no land to which one goes where there is no suffering.
Even if there is a land that is peaceful, secure, and prosperous, if afflictions arise within the mind and cause suffering and distress, it is not a good land;
whereas a land that can eliminate various evils and attenuate the fetters so that the mind is not troubled is called a good land.
All sentient beings have two kinds of suffering:
physical suffering and mental suffering.
There are always sufferings and afflictions; there is no land where these two types of affliction do not exist.

Furthermore, some lands are extremely cold, some lands are extremely hot; some lands suffer from famine, some lands have much disease, some lands have many bandits, and some lands have kings who do not govern according to the Dharma.
"In this way, one should not be attached to the various evils of such realms; by observing correctly in this manner, one eliminates the perception of realms.
He asked: "How does one eliminate the perception of immortality?"

He replied: "One should instruct the practitioner: 'Whether born into a noble family or as the son of a distinguished lineage, do not think at all about your superior talents, skills, strength, or power.'"
Why is this? At the time of death for all beings, [death] does not regard whether one is old or young, noble or lowly, talented or powerful.

This body is the cause and condition for all sorrow and affliction; yet, because of one's own perception of having lived for a short or long duration, or of having attained peace and security, such a person is a fool.
Why is this? Because these are the causes of sorrow and affliction.
Relying upon these four great elements and the form derived from them is like four venomous snakes living together in discord; who could find peace and security therein?
To expect that what has gone out will necessarily come back in is untrustworthy.
Furthermore, when a person sleeps, they may wish to expect that they will certainly wake up, yet this matter is difficult to trust.
From conception until old age, the event of death constantly approaches; while seeking the specific moment of death, one says "I shall not die," so how can this be believed?
For example, it is like a murderous bandit who draws his sword and aims his arrows, constantly seeking to kill people with no heart of compassion.

Among all beings born into this world, death is the greatest force; there is nothing that can surpass the strength of death. Just as in the past no supreme person was able to escape death, so too in the present no one of great wisdom can overcome death. It cannot be avoided by seeking through gentle words, nor can it be evaded by clever speech or deception;
nor can it be repelled by the observance of precepts or diligent effort.

For this reason, you should know that human beings are always precarious and fragile, and cannot be relied upon. Do not believe in the calculation that the self is permanent or that one will live for a long time; these thieves of death are constantly carrying people away, rather than waiting until they have reached old age before killing them.
"Just as an Arhat instructs his disciples who are troubled by various thoughts, saying:
'Why do you not know weariness with the world and enter the Path?
Why do you harbor such thoughts? "

There are those who die before they are even born; there are those who die at the moment of birth; there are those who die while being nursed, those who die when weaned, those who die as infants, those who die in the prime of youth, and those who die in old age. At all times, death pervades the realm of phenomena.
It is like the flowers of a tree: some fall while they are still blossoming, some fall when there are fruits, and some fall before they have ripened.
Therefore, you should know that one must strive with diligence and vigor to seek the path of peace and security; for it is impossible to trust those who dwell together with powerful thieves.
"This thief is like a tiger that skillfully conceals its body; likewise, the thief of death constantly seeks to kill people.
"The entire world is empty, like a water bubble; how can one say that one must wait for the right time to enter the Path?"
Who can testify that you will certainly grow old and still be able to practice the Path?

It is like a great tree on a precipitous bank where a strong wind blows above and a great flood of water erodes its roots and soil below; who would believe that such a tree could remain standing for long?
Human life is also like this: its brevity cannot be trusted.

The father is like the seed of grain; the mother is like a fertile field; the causes and conditions of past lives—whether of sin or merit—are like rain and moisture; sentient beings are like the grain; and birth and death are like the harvest.

The various wisdoms and virtues of the sons of gods and human kings are like those of the celestial king who, assisting the gods in battle, breaks the armies of the asuras; he enjoys manifold pleasures and possesses supreme height and brilliance, yet suddenly sinks back into darkness.
For this reason, do not place trust in the notion that one lives by fate, thinking, "I shall do this today, and I shall do that tomorrow.
By observing such various things correctly, one eliminates the perception of immortality.

"In this way, having first eliminated coarse discursive thoughts and subsequently eliminating subtle discursive thoughts, the mind becomes pure and attains the right path; all fetters and afflictions are exhausted, and from this one attains a state of peace and security—this is called the fruit of renunciation."

Having attained mastery over the mind, with the three karmas being supremely pure, one no longer undergoes rebirth in a womb; by reading various sūtras and possessing great learning, one then attains the fruit of retribution.
When one attains this state, the army of Māra is not in vain defeated, and one immediately gains the foremost reputation for valor.
To merely drive away the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the world is not called being "heroic";

rather, it is only when one can destroy the thieves of affliction, extinguish the fires of the three poisons, and attain the cool bliss of purity—resting peacefully on a high pillow within the forest of *nirvāṇa*, with the various dhyānas, faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) like a rising breeze from all sides—that one is truly heroic. To look back with compassion upon sentient beings submerged in the sea of the three poisons, possessing such wondrous power of virtue, is what is called being "heroic."

In such states of distracted mind, one should practice *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and train in the six methods to sever discursive thoughts; for this reason, one practices counting the breaths.

Question: "If discursive thoughts can also be severed within other practices—such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*)—why is counting the breaths alone [prescribed]?"
He replied: "Because other methods of contemplation are broad and difficult to lose, whereas the method of counting breaths is urgent and easily shifted.

It is like tending cattle: because cattle are difficult to lose, guarding them requires little effort; whereas tending monkeys is easy for them to escape, guarding them requires much effort. This is just the same!"

In counting the breaths, the mind must not entertain other thoughts for even a moment; if one entertains other thoughts for a moment, the count is lost. For this reason, at the outset, one should sever discursive thoughts by counting the breaths.
Having attained the method of counting, one should practice the method of following; one should sever all discursive thoughts. When inhaling to the end, one should follow it without counting "one";
when exhaling to the end, one should follow it without counting "two."
For example, it is like a debtor whom a creditor pursues and never lets go.
One reflects in this way: "Is this the inhalation, or is there something different that returns as exhalation?"
Is there any difference between exhalation and inhalation?
At that time, one knows that inhalation is distinct and exhalation is distinct. Why is this so?
The exhalation is warm; the inhalation is cool.
Question: "Inhalation and exhalation constitute a single breath."
Why is this? Because the exhaled breath returns and enters again.
It is like water held in the mouth: if it is warm when held, it becomes cold when spat out; that which was cold becomes warm again, and that which was warm becomes cold again.
He replied: "No!
Because the internal mind moves, there is the exhalation of breath; once it has been exhaled, it immediately ceases."
When the nose and mouth draw [air] outward, there is inhalation; because it enters, the breath ceases, such that there is neither that which is about to go out nor that which is about to enter.

Furthermore, among the young, the middle-aged, and the elderly: for the young, inhalation is long; for the middle-aged, inhalation and exhalation are equal; for the elderly, exhalation is long. Therefore, it is not a single breath.
Furthermore, the wind arising at the navel proceeds in a continuous succession; it exits through the mouth and nostrils, and having exited, it immediately ceases.
It is like the air within a bellows, which ceases as soon as [the bellows] is opened.
If one draws it in by means of the mouth and nose as conditions, then wind enters; this arises from the side of new conditions.
It is like a fan: because various conditions combine, there is wind.
At that time, one understands that the causes and conditions of inhalation and exhalation are deceptive and unreal, subject to arising and ceasing, and impermanent.

Reflecting in this way, one realizes that exhalation arises from being drawn forth by the conditions of the mouth and nose, while inhalation is produced by the movement of the mind; yet the deluded do not know this, taking them instead to be "my breaths."
"Exhalation is wind; it is no different from external wind. Earth, water, fire, and space are likewise!
Because of the combination of these five great elements as causes and conditions, consciousness arises. Consciousness is also like this: it does not belong to a self!"
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are also like this!
To know them thus, following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath—this is why it is called "following" (anupassanā).
Having already attained the practice that accords with the Dharma, one should now practice the method of cessation.

As for the method of cessation: it consists of counting and following the mind to its limit, fixing the attention at the gate of the breath, and maintaining mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation. Question:
"Why does one cease? He replied:
"Because all discursive thoughts and perceptions are severed, and the mind is not distracted."
"When counting while following the breath, the mind is unsettled because it is overly active;
when stopping, the mind becomes leisurely because there are few activities and it abides in one place.
To be mindful of the inhalation and exhalation is like a gatekeeper standing by the gate, observing people entering and exiting.
The settling of the mind is likewise!
One knows that when the breath goes out, it proceeds from the navel, the heart, the chest, and the throat to the mouth and nose.
When the breath comes in, it proceeds from the mouth and nose, through the throat, the chest, and the heart, to the navel.
Thus binding the mind to a single point is called *śamatha*.
Furthermore, while abiding in the method of mental cessation, one practices *vipaśyanā*.

At the time of inhaling, the five aggregates arise and cease differently; at the time of exhaling, the five aggregates arise and cease differently. In this way, mental distraction is eliminated, and by contemplating with a single-minded focus, one causes insight to increase; this is called the method of *vipaśyanā*.

Leaving the gateway of the wind and abiding in the dharma of contemplation free from coarseness, one knows through this contemplation free from coarseness that the breath is impermanent; this is called "transformative contemplation.
One contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, and likewise contemplates the arising and ceasing—and thus the impermanence—of inhalation and exhalation.

Observe that the initial inhalation comes from nowhere; next, observe that the subsequent exhalation likewise leaves no trace. It exists because causes and conditions converge, and it ceases because causes and conditions disperse. This is called the method of progressive observation.

Having eliminated the five hindrances and all afflictions, although one previously attained serenity and insight, the mind was still defiled by impure afflictions; now, through this pure dharma, the mind alone attains complete purity.

Furthermore, previously one observed the inhalation and exhalation of breath while practicing a path similar to that of the heterodox teachers; now, one practices a wholesome path with outflows that is similar to the untainted (anāsrava) path—this is called purification.

Furthermore, first one contemplates the stage of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), gradually attaining full mindfulness of the body; next, one practices mindfulness of feelings and the mind (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna* and *citta-smṛtyupasthāna*). Within these, there is no purity, because they are far removed from the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).

Now, within the station of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates the sixteen aspects while attending to the inhalation and exhalation; thereby one attains the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). From the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhadharmakṣānti*) up to the Knowledge of Exhaustion of the One Beyond Training (*aśaikṣakṣayajñāna*), this is called purification.
Within these sixteen steps, the first six types of *ānāpāna* practice pertain to the inhalation; the exhalation is likewise.

With single-minded mindfulness, one contemplates whether the inhalation and exhalation are long or short: for example, if a person runs up a mountain in fear, or carries a heavy burden, or is out of breath—such as these, the breath is short;
if a person, at a time of extreme exhaustion, attains rest and joy, or gains a profit, or is released from prison—such as these, the breath is long.
All breaths follow two locations:
either the long or the short location; therefore, one speaks of "long breath" and "short breath.

Within this, one also practices the six matters of *ānāpāna*: mindfulness that the breath pervades the entire body, mindfulness of the inhalation and exhalation, and observing all the out-breaths and in-breaths within the body, perceiving them reaching everywhere throughout the body down to the tips of the toes, pervading all the pores like water entering sand.
One perceives the exhalation as it proceeds from the feet up to the hair, pervading all the pores like water entering sand.
It is like a bellows that is full both when drawing in and when expelling; the inhalation and exhalation of wind through the mouth and nose is likewise so.
One contemplates the body in its entirety, observing the places where the winds circulate, like the holes in a lotus root or the mesh of a fishing net.

Furthermore, it is not only through the mouth and nose that one observes the inhalation and exhalation of breath; one also observes the inhalation and exhalation within all the pores and the nine apertures.
Therefore, one knows that the breath pervades the entire body; one eliminates all bodily formations and remains mindful of the inhalation and exhalation.
When first practicing the breath, if there is physical lethargy, drowsiness, or heaviness, one must completely discard them!
The body becomes light and supple; following the mind of meditative concentration, one experiences joy, while also being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
One eliminates sloth, torpor, and mental heaviness, attaining a state where the mind is light and supple, and follows the mind of meditative concentration to experience joy.
Furthermore, having completed the application of mindfulness to inhalation, one next practices the application of mindfulness to sensation;
having already attained the application of mindfulness to the body, one now truly further attains the application of mindfulness to sensation and truly experiences joy.

Furthermore, having already understood the true nature of the body, one now wishes to understand the true nature of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*). For this reason, one experiences joy while being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, and one experiences pleasure while being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; this increase of joy is what is called pleasure.
Furthermore, the joy that arises in the initial moment of mind is called *prīti* (rapture), while the subsequent joy that pervades the entire body is called *sukha* (bliss).

Furthermore, the sensation of pleasure within the first and second dhyānas is called *prīti*, whereas the sensation of pleasure within the third dhyāna is called the experience of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*).
One experiences all mental activities, while also being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.

All phenomena of the arising and ceasing of the mind—phenomena of mental defilement and non-defilement, phenomena of mental distraction and concentration, and phenomena of mental correctness and error—such as these various characteristics of the mind are called "mental activities" (*cittasamskāra*).

When the mind produces joy, one also contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath—first experiencing the spontaneous arising of joy, rather than intentionally forming the thought, "the mind shall intentionally produce joy.
Question: "For what reason does one intentionally produce joy?"
He replied: "I wish to discipline two kinds of mind:
either the distracted mind or the concentrated mind."
By forming the mind in this way, one escapes from afflictions; therefore, one contemplates the Dharma, and the mind gives rise to joy.
Furthermore, if the mind is not joyful, one should encourage and exhort it until it becomes joyful.
When the mind is being gathered, one also contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath—if the mind is not concentrated, one forcibly subdues it to bring it to concentration.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"A concentrated mind is the Path; a distracted mind is not the Path."
When the mind attains liberation, one likewise maintains mindfulness of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; if the mind is not liberated, one forcibly subdues it until it is liberated.
It is like a sheep entering a field of cockleburs: when the cockleburs stick to its body, people gradually pull them out for it.
The mind’s liberation from the fetters of all afflictions is likewise so!
This is called the liberation through the application of mindfulness to the mind.

One also contemplates impermanence while being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation—contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, empty, and devoid of a self. When they arise, all phenomena arise as empty; when they cease, all phenomena cease as empty. Within this, there is no male, no female, no person, no agent, and no experiencer. This is called the contemplation in accordance with impermanence.

Contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as emerging and dispersing, and likewise the mindfulness of the inhalation and exhalation of breath—impermanence is what is called "emerging and dispersing.

All conditioned phenomena emerge within the present world; they accumulate because of the conjunction of past causes and conditions, and they disperse because those causes and conditions perish. To contemplate in this manner is called the contemplation of emerging and dispersing.

Contemplating the departure from the fetters, one is also mindful of the inhalation and exhalation—when the mind is detached from all fetters, this is the foremost dharma; this is called the contemplation following departure.

Contemplating cessation, one is also mindful of the inhalation and exhalation—wherever the suffering of the various fetters and latent tendencies ceases, that place is secure; this is called the contemplation following cessation.

Contemplating relinquishment while also being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, one relinquishes all defiled cravings, afflictions, the five aggregates of body and mind, and all conditioned phenomena; this is the foremost state of peace and security.
Contemplating in this manner is called "mindfulness of dharmas according to the Dharma" (dharmānusmṛti-samādhi); this is termed the sixteen aspects.

Regarding the fifth dharma gate for treating those of equal dispositions: for those of equal disposition and those who have committed grave offenses seeking the Buddha, such persons should be taught the single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha-samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
There are three types of persons regarding the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha:
those who have newly begun their practice, those who have already practiced it, and those who have long practiced it.

As for the person who has newly begun their practice, when they approach the place where a Buddha image is located, they are instructed either to go there themselves and attentively contemplate the marks and signs of the Buddha’s physical excellence until each mark is clearly perceived, or to single-mindedly grasp and maintain that visualization.

Returning to a quiet place, one contemplates the Buddha-image with the mind’s eye, ensuring that the mind does not wander. One binds mindfulness to the image and does not allow other thoughts to arise;
if other thoughts do arise, one restrains them so that mindfulness remains constantly upon the image.
If the mind does not abide, the teacher should instruct him, saying:
"You must reproach yourself:
'Because of you, you have undergone incalculable sins; throughout boundless births and deaths, there is no kind of suffering that you have not experienced.'"
If one is in hell, one swallows molten copper and eats glowing iron balls;
if one is among the animals, one eats excrement and chews grass;
if one is among the hungry ghosts, one undergoes the suffering of hunger.
If among humans, you cause poverty and distress;
if in the heavens, you cause the loss of desires and mental anguish.
Because you constantly follow me, you have caused me to undergo these various physical and mental afflictions, and immeasurable sufferings.
"I shall now subdue you; you must follow me.
I will now bind you in one place, so that I shall never again be oppressed by you nor suffer further bitter torment."
"You have always troubled me; now I must trouble you with a matter.

When he spoke thus without ceasing, his mind remained undistracted, and at that moment he attained the eye of the mind and beheld the marks and radiance of the Buddha’s image, no different from what is seen by the physical eye.
When the mind abides in this way, it is called the contemplation of a beginner practitioner.
At that time, one should further reflect, saying:
"What is the characteristic of this image?"
This is the physical form of the past Buddha Śākyamuni.
Just as I now see the image of the Buddha, the image does not come to me, nor do I go to it.
Thus, with such mental visualization, one sees the past Buddha when he first descended into his mother’s womb, causing heaven and earth to tremble.
There are thirty-two marks of a Great Man:
first, the soles of the feet stand flat and level;
second, there are wheels with a thousand spokes on the soles of the feet.
Third, his fingers are long and beautiful.
Fourth, his heels are broad.
Fifth, his fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane.
Sixth, his instep is high, level, and beautiful.
Seventh, his calves are like those of the eneya deer.
Eighth, standing upright, his hands reach below his knees.
Ninth, the mark of the sheathed organ like that of a horse;
tenth, the body like that of the nyagrodha tree;
eleventh, a single hair growing from each pore.
Twelfth, the body hairs grow upward and curl to the right.
Thirteenth, the color of the body is superior to refined gold.
Fourteenth, the radiance of the body extends one zhang in every direction.
Fifteenth, his skin is thin and fine.
Sixteenth, he is full in seven places.
Seventeenth, both armpits are level and well-formed.
Eighteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion.
Nineteenth, his body is large, beautiful, and perfectly straight.
Twentieth, his shoulders are rounded and well-formed.
Twenty-first: he has forty teeth. Twenty-second:
his teeth are white, even, closely set, uniform, and deeply rooted.
Twenty-third: his four canine teeth are white and large.
Twenty-fourth, his cheeks are square like those of a lion.
Twenty-fifth, he attains the supreme taste among all tastes.
Twenty-sixth, his tongue is large, broad, long, and thin.
Twenty-seventh, his Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching.
Twenty-eighth, he has the voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
Twenty-ninth, his eyes are a deep azure-blue.
Thirtieth: his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
Thirty-first: the hair on his crown is formed of flesh and bone.
Thirty-second: between his eyebrows there is a white hair, long and beautiful, curling to the right.
Furthermore, there are eighty secondary marks:
first, the crown of the head is invisible;
second, the nose is straight, high, and well-formed, with the nostrils not visible.
Third, his eyebrows are like the newly risen crescent moon, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.
Fourth, his ears are beautiful.
Fifth, his body is like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Sixth, the joints of his bones are like interlocking hooks.
Seventh, when he turns his body, it does so all at once like an elephant king.
Eighth, when he walks, his feet leave the ground four inches while the marks of his feet appear.
Ninth, his nails are the color of red copper, thin and glossy.
Tenth, his knees are perfectly rounded.
Eleventh, his body is pure and clean.
Twelfth, his body is supple.
Thirteenth, his body is not crooked.
Fourteenth, his fingers are long, rounded, and slender.
Fifteenth, the fingerprints are like paintings, adorned with various colors.
Sixteenth, the veins are deep and do not appear.
Seventeenth, the ankles are deep and do not appear.
Eighteenth, his body is moist and radiant.
Nineteenth, his body is self-sustained and does not lean or collapse.
Twentieth, his body is fully developed; he was conceived for three months and born after two months [of gestation].
Twenty-first, his deportment is fully perfected.
Twenty-second, he stands as firm and immovable as a bull-king in his dwelling place.
Twenty-third, his majestic power vibrates throughout all things.
Twenty-fourth, he delights in all things.
Twenty-fifth, his face is not long.
Twenty-sixth, his countenance is upright and his expression is never distorted.
Twenty-seventh, his lips are the color of the *bimba* fruit.
Twenty-eighth, his face is perfectly round.
Twenty-ninth, his voice is deep.
Thirtieth: the navel is round, deep, and does not protrude.
Thirty-first: the body hairs curl to the right at every point.
Thirty-second: the hands and feet are full and well-filled.
Thirty-third, his hands and feet are supple and compliant—what was formerly called "the inner and outer grasping.
Thirty-fourth, the lines on his hands and feet are distinct, bright, and straight.
Thirty-fifth, the lines on his palms are long.
Thirty-sixth, the lines on his palms are unbroken.
Thirty-seventh, all sentient beings with evil minds who behold him attain a serene and joyful countenance.
Thirty-eighth, his face is broad and beautiful.
Thirty-ninth, his face is like the moon.
Fortieth, sentient beings who see him feel neither fear nor dread.
Forty-first, fragrant winds issue from his pores.
Forty-second: His mouth emits a fragrant aroma such that any sentient being who encounters it delights in the Dharma for seven days.
Forty-third: His deportment is like that of a lion.
Forty-fourth: His gait and movements are like those of an elephant king.
Forty-fifth: His gait is like that of a king of geese.
Forty-sixth: His head is like a madhura fruit—this fruit being neither round nor long.
Forty-seventh: His vocal qualities are complete; his voice possesses sixty distinct qualities, all of which the Buddha fully possesses.
Forty-eighth, his canine teeth are sharp.
Forty-ninth, because there is no corresponding name in the Han language, [this mark] cannot be expressed.
Fiftieth, his tongue is broad and red.
Fifty-first, his tongue is thin.
Fifty-second, his body hairs are purely red in color and clean and bright.
Fifty-third, his eyes are wide and long.
Fifty-fourth, his nine apertures are complete and fully endowed with their characteristic marks.
