Fifty-fifth, his hands and feet are reddish-white, like the color of a lotus flower.
Fifty-sixth, his abdomen is neither sunken nor protruding.
Fifty-seventh, his abdomen is not bulging.
Fifty-eighth, he does not move his body.
Fifty-ninth: heavy body. Sixtieth: large body. Sixty-first: tall body.
Sixty-second, his hands and feet are full and pure.
Sixty-third, a great light radiates from all four sides, and he walks while illuminating himself with that brilliance.
Sixty-fourth, he regards all sentient beings with equanimity.
Sixty-fifth: not being attached to teaching others nor coveting disciples.
Sixty-sixth: conforming to the voices of the assembly, neither diminishing nor exceeding them.
Sixty-seventh: preaching the Dharma in accordance with the sounds and voices of the assembly.
Sixty-eighth: his speech is unimpeded.
Sixty-ninth: he preaches the Dharma in a continuous succession.
Seventieth: no sentient being can gaze upon him with their eyes and fully comprehend his appearance.
Seventy-first: his gaze is never satiated.
Seventy-second: his hair is long and beautiful.
Seventy-third: his hair is excellent.
Seventy-fourth, his hair is not disheveled.
Seventy-fifth, his hair is not broken.
Seventy-sixth, his hair is soft and supple.
Seventy-seventh: his hair is the color of blue *vaiḍūrya*.
Seventy-eighth: his hair is bound upward.
Seventy-ninth: his hair is not thin.

Eighty: His chest bears the mark of virtue, and his hands and feet bear the marks of auspiciousness. His radiance shines through immeasurable worlds; at birth, he takes seven steps and utters essential words.

He leaves the household life to practice asceticism, and beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdues the demonic armies. At the break of dawn during the final watch of the night, he attains Equal and Right Enlightenment. His radiant marks are distinct, shining far throughout the ten directions without exception. The various devas in the sky offer praise with stringed songs and provide offerings, scattering flowers and raining down incense. All sentient beings pay him boundless respect. Walking alone through the three realms, he turns his body back as an elephant king turns its head, gazing upon the Bodhi tree. When he first turns the Wheel of Dharma, gods and humans attain awakening; through the Way, they personally realize the attainment of Nirvana.
The Buddha’s body is thus; it inspires immeasurable [faith]. One should concentrate the mind on mindfulness of the Buddha and not allow external thoughts to arise;
should external thoughts of various conditions occur, one should collect them and bring them back [to the Buddha].

Being thus undistracted, one then comes to see the form-bodies of one Buddha, two Buddhas, and even the Buddhas of immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions; because of the power of mental visualization, one sees them all, and having seen the Buddhas, one further hears their words as they preach the Dharma.
Or one may personally inquire of the Buddha, who will preach the Dharma for them to untangle the net of all doubts.

Having attained mindfulness of the Buddha, one should further contemplate the Buddha’s meritorious qualities: his Dharma-body, his immeasurable great wisdom, his boundless and unfathomable knowledge, and his incalculable virtues.
*Tathāgata*: *Tathā* is translated into the Qin language as "thus" (*ru*).
*Āgata* means "come" (*jie*), or it means "truthful speech" (*shiyu*); it also means that while other sages have come by way of the path of peace, the Buddha has come in such a manner;
furthermore, he will not come again into a future existence. *Arhant*: *Ari* (pronounced with the *lu-mi* rhyme) is translated into the Qin language as "thief."
"Ha" means "to kill.

The Buddha takes patience as his armor, diligence as his sturdy shield, meditative concentration as his bow, and wisdom as his arrow; he kills the thieves of pride and the like, and is therefore called "Killer of Thieves" (Arhat). *Samyak-saṃbuddha*: *Samyak* (pronounced with a retroflex *c*) means "true" or "reality" in the language of Qin.
A *Saṃbuddha* is called "one who awakens to all.

He awakens to suffering and its cause (*samudaya*), and to nirvāṇa and its cause (*mārga*). Through correct understanding, he perceives the four truths as unshakeable; having realized them exhaustively without remainder, he is therefore said to be "truly awakened to all. *Vidyā* (pronounced *bi-qié*, with *yè* reversed) is translated into Chinese as "clarity" (*ming*).
*Śīla* (遮羅那) means "good conduct. It refers to the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

Because one performs pure conduct and thereby alone achieves the great enlightenment without a teacher, it is called "clear knowledge and good conduct. *Sampanna* (三般那) is translated in the Qin language as "fulfillment. *Sugata* (宿伽陀) is translated in the Qin language as "well-understood," also named "well-attained by oneself," and further described as "well-spoken and free from affliction. *Lokavid* (路伽憊)—the character *lù* is pronounced with the *pí* rhyme—is translated in the Qin language as "wisdom."
The wise one knows the causes of the world and knows the path to its cessation; therefore, he is called "World-Knower" (*loka-jña*).
World-knowledge means knowing the world. *Anuttara*—in the language of Qin, it means "unsurpassed.

His wholesome dharmas and noble wisdom guide all beings; his great virtue is immeasurable, such that neither Brahmā, Māra, nor any of the assembly of sages can equal him, let alone surpass the Buddha, whose virtues are supreme and vast.
Therefore, he is called "Unsurpassed" (Anuttara). *Puruṣadamyasārathi*: *puruṣa* in the language of Qin means "great man" (*mahāpuruṣa*);
*damya* means one who can be spoken to, one who can be transformed—a man who is a teacher and tamer.

Because the Buddha possesses great kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom, he at times uses gentle and beautiful speech, and at other times uses harsh and piercing speech; or he may provide direct instruction. By means of these methods, he tames and guides beings so that they do not lose the Way; therefore, the Buddha is called the "Great Man Capable of Transformation" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) and the "Dharma of the Tamer. *Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*: *śāstā* is pronounced with the initial sound of *she-xie* (捨賒) and the final *du-è* (都餓); *deva-manuṣyāṇām* has the initial *nu-gan* (奴甘); in the language of Qin, this means "Teacher of Gods and Humans."

He is fully able to liberate all people from their afflictions and eternally abides in the supreme Dharma from which there is no regression. Regarding the past, future, and present, the Buddha Bhagavān knows what has been practiced and what has not been practiced, and what is exhausted and what is not exhausted; he clearly and completely understands all phenomena beneath the Bodhi tree. For this reason, he is named Buddha Bhagavān.
It is said:
"There is a great name and fame.
Furthermore, the term *vā* refers to the female organ (*strīndriya*).
The name "Po" (婆) means "to vomit.
Because one eternally abandons the female organ, it is called the "vomiting of the female organ.
At that time, one further recollects the divine virtues of two Buddhas, three, four, five, or even immeasurable Buddhas throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space; all are exactly like this.

Furthermore, they again see one Buddha; they are able to see one Buddha manifest as the Buddhas of the ten directions, and they are able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest as one Buddha.
They can cause a single color to become the colors of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli, causing all to see them according to their own inclinations and desires.
At that time, one contemplates only two things:

the space-like Buddha-body and the Buddha’s merits. Without any other thoughts, the mind attains mastery and the intellect does not wander; at this moment, one achieves the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
If the mind wanders and scatters, with thoughts fixed upon the five sensory objects or the six modes of perception, one should exhort and strenuously discipline the mind, forcibly subduing it!
Reflecting thus on how difficult it is to obtain a human body and how rare it is to encounter the Buddha-dharma, it is said:
"Among all luminaries, the sun is supreme; among all forms of wisdom, the Buddha is supreme."

Why is this? The Buddha has given rise to great compassion and constantly acts for the sake of all beings; he has even offered his head, eyes, marrow, and brain to rescue and deliver sentient beings. How could one set their mind at ease, failing to focus single-mindedly on the Buddha and thus betraying such profound kindness?
If a Buddha did not appear in the world, there would be no path to the human realm, no path to the heavenly realms, and no path to Nirvana.

Even if one were to offer incense and flowers, or construct stupas with bones, flesh, blood, and marrow as offerings, these would not equal the merit of a practitioner who offers the Dharma and thereby attains Nirvana.

Although one still bears the Buddha’s kindness, even if recollecting the Buddha were to yield no results whatsoever, one should still diligently and single-mindedly maintain mindfulness without forgetfulness in order to repay that kindness; how much more so when recollecting the Buddha leads to the attainment of various samādhis, wisdom, and the realization of Buddhahood—how could one not be single-minded in this recollection?

Therefore, a practitioner should always concentrate their mind so that it does not become distracted; having attained the vision of the Buddha, they should request clarification on whatever doubts they may have. This is called the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
It eradicates the "equal-parts" afflictions as well as other grave offenses.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation, Volume Upper;
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation, Volume Lower.
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
At that time, although the practitioner has attained one-pointedness of mind, their power of concentration is not yet perfected;
they remain disturbed by the afflictions of the desire realm and should therefore employ skillful means to advance in the study of the first dhyāna, rebuking and abandoning craving and desire.
How does one rebuke and abandon them?
One contemplates the faults of the desire realm, seeing that desire is impure and variously unwholesome;
one should then mindfully recollect the first dhyāna, which is peaceful, secure, and blissful.
Regarding the contemplation of desire: how does one know that desire is impermanent?

It is a source of merit and enmity, like an illusion or a magical transformation; it is empty and unattainable. If the mind is already disturbed by the mere thought of it before it is obtained, how much more so when it is actually attained and one is shrouded by the fetters of lustful desire?
Even the blissful realms of the heavens are not eternally secure, let alone those among human beings.
The human mind is attached to desire and knows no satiety; it is like fire obtaining fuel, or as the ocean swallows flowing streams.
For example, King Mūrdhaja, though he rained down the seven treasures, ruled over the four continents, and shared a seat with Śakra, was still not satisfied.
Likewise, Nahuṣa (by clan), who was a wheel-turning monarch, was driven by desire and fell among the pythons.
Furthermore, it is like the rishis who eat fruit and wear grass, dwelling in deep mountains with disheveled hair seeking the Way; yet even they cannot avoid being destroyed by the thieves of desire.
Sensual pleasures are few, while enmity and poison are many.
For one who clings to desire, evil friends draw near while virtuous people remain distant.
Desire is like a poisonous wine; the deluded and ignorant become intoxicated and die.
Desire acts as a deception, driving fools about and subjecting them to myriad forms of exhaustion and suffering, depriving them of self-mastery.
Only by abandoning desire does one attain peace and stability of body and mind, leading to unsurpassed bliss.
Desire yields nothing; it is like a dog gnawing on a dry bone.
One exerts oneself in the pursuit of desire until extreme suffering ensues; it is very difficult to obtain and very easy to lose.
Like a temporary loan, its momentum cannot endure; like what is seen in a dream, it vanishes in a blur.
Desire is a source of affliction: seeking it is suffering, and obtaining it is also suffering; the more one obtains, the more suffering one encounters.
Just as fire gains fuel and grows ever more intense, desire is like a piece of meat that birds vie to seize.
To speak in brief:
it is like a moth rushing into a flame, a fish swallowing a hook, a deer chasing a sound, or a thirsty person drinking salt water.
All sentient beings, because they pursue desire, bring about affliction; there is no suffering to which they do not succumb.
Therefore, one should know that desire is a poisonous harm; one should seek the first dhyāna to extinguish and sever the fire of desire.

The practitioner, with single-minded diligence, faith, and joy, causes the mind to progress and the intellect to remain undistracted; contemplating the mind’s aversion to desire, they exhaust all fetters and afflictions and attain the first dhyāna-concentration.
Having escaped the blazing fire of desire, they obtain a cool concentration, like one who finds shade in the heat, or like a poor person who attains wealth.
At that time, one attains the joy of the first dhyāna; while contemplating the various merits within the dhyāna and discerning the beautiful and the ugly, one then attains single-mindedness.
Question: "When a practitioner of dhyāna attains the mark of one-pointedness of mind, how can it be known? Answer:

"His countenance is radiant and smooth; he walks slowly and with steady composure, never losing his single-minded focus. His eyes do not cling to forms; through the power of his spiritual virtue and meditative concentration, he does not crave fame or profit. Having shattered arrogance, his nature is gentle and supple; he harbors no malice and is free from stinginess or envy. With a straightforward mind and pure faith, he does not engage in contentious debate. His body is free from deceit, making him easy to converse with.

Gentle and possessing a sense of shame and remorse, his mind always dwells upon the Dharma. He cultivates diligence with vigor, maintains the precepts in their entirety, recites the sutras with correct mindfulness, and follows the practice of the Dharma in every thought.

His mind is constantly joyful, and he does not give way to anger even when provoked. Among the four types of offerings, he does not accept what is impure, but accepts pure gifts; he knows moderation and is content."
Upon waking, one is alert and agile, capable of practicing the two kinds of giving; through patience, one eliminates deviance; in debate, one is not self-satisfied; and one’s speech is sparing.
One is humble and reverent toward those of superior, middling, and inferior seats; one constantly draws near to and follows virtuous teachers and spiritual friends;

one knows moderation in food and drink and does not cling to the flavors of desire; one delights in solitary, quiet places; whether in suffering or pleasure, the mind remains patient and unmoved; one is without resentment or rivalry, and takes no pleasure in strife or litigation.
"Through such various signs as these, one comes to know the characteristic of a single-minded state.

These two factors, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), disturb the mind in meditative concentration; it is like clear, still water that becomes turbid when ruffled by waves. For the practitioner, having attained internal one-pointedness, they are nonetheless troubled by vitarka and vicāra, just as one who has found extreme rest is disturbed by the movement of sleep, or as one who has attained peace is disturbed by dreaming.

At that time, with the sequential cessation of applied and sustained thought, he gives rise to pure concentration, characterized by internal purity, joy, and bliss, and thus attains the second dhyāna.
His mind becomes tranquil and silent; this joy, which was previously unattainable, he now attains.

At that time, observing the mind, one perceives joy as a source of affliction; as in the aforementioned contemplation, one practices the dharma of non-joy and thus leaves the stage of joy. One attains the bliss spoken of by the noble ones, and with single-minded clarity, mindfulness, and protection, enters the third dhyāna.

Having already abandoned joy, one clearly knows and mindfully maintains this blissful protection; what the Noble Ones call "blissful protection" is difficult for others to relinquish, and it is the foremost among all forms of bliss. Beyond this, there is no further bliss.
Therefore, among all pure stages, the noble ones declare loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to be the foremost bliss.
Yet bliss is itself a source of affliction. Why is this so?

In the first dhyāna, the mind does not waver because there is no cause for disturbance; where there is wavering, there is fluctuation, and where there is fluctuation, there is suffering. Therefore, in the third dhyāna, bliss is regarded as a source of affliction.

Furthermore, by means of excellent equanimity, one abandons both pleasure and pain; having previously cast off sorrow and joy, one dwells with an intention free from pleasure and pain, attaining the pure mindfulness and equanimity of the fourth dhyāna.
Being neither in pain nor in pleasure, one possesses pure mindfulness and single-mindedness. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"The most pure equanimity is supreme; this is called the fourth dhyāna."
Because the bliss of the third dhyāna is subject to movement, it is designated as suffering; therefore, the fourth dhyāna eliminates both suffering and bliss and is called the "unmoving state.

One gradually contemplates the sphere of infinite space, breaking down the perception of internal and external form, extinguishing the perception of resistance, and no longer attending to perceptions of diverse forms;
one contemplates the sphere of infinite space while constantly observing the defects of form.
One contemplates the sublime and excellent qualities of the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
By practicing mindfulness of this dharma, one attains the sphere of infinite space.
One then contemplates the sphere of infinite consciousness, observing the defects of the sphere of infinite space and reflecting upon the qualities of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
By practicing mindfulness of this dharma, one attains the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana).
One contemplates the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), observing the defects of the sphere of consciousness and reflecting upon the merits of the sphere of nothingness.
By practicing mindfulness of this dharma, one then attains the sphere of nothingness.

One contemplates the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, [reflecting]: "If there were all manner of perceptions, their afflictions would be manifold—like diseases or like sores; yet if there were no perception, that would be a state of delusion."
Therefore, the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the foremost secure and auspicious place.

By contemplating the faults of the sphere of nothingness and recollecting the merits of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one practices mindfulness of this dharma and thereby attains the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

There may be a practitioner who, having first proceeded from the first stage up to the higher stages, further cultivates the practice of a compassionate mind within those higher stages; first attaining happiness for themselves and destroying the poison of anger, they subsequently extend it to immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
At that time, he immediately attained the samādhi of loving-kindness.
With a heart of compassion, he took pity on the suffering of sentient beings, being able to destroy all afflictions and extending his reach widely to immeasurable beings.
At that time, he attains the samādhi of compassion,
which is able to destroy displeasure and cause immeasurable sentient beings to all attain joy.
At that time, he attains the samādhi of sympathetic joy.

Being able to transcend suffering and pleasure, one directly contemplates the immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions; at that time, one immediately attains the Samādhi of the Protective Mind.
The second dhyāna is likewise, while in the third and fourth dhyanas, joy is eliminated.
Next, one studies the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), whereby the body is able to fly and transformations are performed with mastery.
The practitioner, with single-mindedness, cultivates the concentration of desire, the concentration of diligence, the concentration of single-mindedness, and the concentration of wisdom.

With single-mindedness, one contemplates the body and constantly cultivates the perception of lightness, desiring to achieve the power of flight. Whether [the body] becomes large or small—becoming large through the excess of desire-concentration (*kāmadhyāna*) and becoming small through its deficiency—one encounters these two faults. Yet, through diligent and tireless effort, being able to maintain single-mindedness and contemplate the perception of lightness, it is like a person who can float:
because the power of the mind is strong, they do not sink; or like a monkey falling from a height: because the power of the mind is strong, the body suffers no pain.

It is the same in this case: by causing the power of desire, the power of diligence, the power of single-mindedness, and the power of wisdom to expand, while the body becomes smaller, one is then able to transport the body.
Furthermore, one contemplates the empty element of the body.

By constantly practicing this contemplation, the power of desire, the power of diligence, the power of single-mindedness, and the power of wisdom become exceedingly vast, whereby one is able to lift the entire body.
Just as the power of a great wind can carry heavy objects to a great distance, so it is with this!
One should first test oneself by rising one or two feet off the ground, gradually increasing to ten feet, and then returning to the original spot.
It is like a fledgling bird learning to fly or a small child learning to walk; by reflecting and examining oneself, one knows that the power of the mind is great and that it will surely reach far.

When practicing the contemplation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), if one sets aside the earth element and contemplates only the other three, and the mental focus remains undistracted, one immediately attains mastery. The body becomes free from obstruction, just like a bird in flight.
One should further practice this: by conceiving of the distant as near, that which is near is extinguished and that which is distant emerges.
Furthermore, one can transform various objects; for example, if one contemplates the wood-element within the earth-element and eliminates all other elements, this wood will then transform into earth.
Why is this so? Because wood possesses the constituent element of earth.
Water, fire, wind, space, gold, silver, and precious objects are all likewise.
Why is this? Because wood possesses various constituent parts.
This is the fundamental basis for the first supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
In the fourth dhyāna, there are fourteen transformational minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*);
in the first dhyāna, there are two fruits:
the first is the first dhyāna itself.
Second, the desire realm. Regarding the three fruits of the second dhyāna:
first, the second dhyāna itself.
Second is the first dhyāna;
third is the desire realm.
The three dhyānas and the four fruits:
First, the third dhyāna;
second, the second dhyāna;
third, the first dhyāna.
Fourth is the realm of desire.
Regarding the four dhyānas and five fruits:
first are the four dhyānas.
Second, the third dhyāna; third, the second dhyāna;
fourth, the first dhyāna.
Fifth is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The remaining [realms] are common [to all], as explained in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*.
Among the disciples of the World-Honored One who train in these five dharma-gates with the resolve to seek nirvāṇa, there are two types of persons:
Some prefer concentration more, because of its bliss;
others prefer wisdom more, out of fear of suffering and affliction.
Those who prefer concentration first study the methods of dhyāna, and subsequently study nirvāṇa.
Those with great wisdom proceed directly toward *nirvāṇa*.

To proceed directly toward *nirvāṇa* means that, although one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one focuses the mind without distraction to seek *nirvāṇa* directly; by transcending craving and all other afflictions, this is called *nirvāṇa*.
The body is in truth impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self; yet, because the mind is inverted, one perceives it as permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure.
For this reason, one becomes attached to the body in every respect; such a person is a base being.
In order to destroy perversions, the practitioner should practice the four foundations of mindfulness through both calm abiding and insight:
observing that the body is manifold and beset by many sufferings;

that it is impermanent because it arises from causes and conditions; that it is suffering because it is subject to various afflictions; that it is impure because it consists of thirty-six substances; and that it is non-self because it lacks autonomy.

Practicing such contemplation—contemplating the internal body, contemplating the external body, and contemplating both the internal and external body—and practicing such contemplation is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Such is the true nature of the body!
For what reason does one give rise to inverted attachment toward this body?

Reflect with careful attention: regarding the body, self, pleasure, and pain, it is because of attachment to pleasure and pain that one clings to this body; one should observe that pleasure and pain are in reality unobtainable.
How is it that one cannot derive pleasure from clothing and food?
When pleasure passes, suffering arises, for it is not true pleasure.
It is like the pain of a wound: when it is treated by applying medicine, the cessation of the pain is taken as pleasure.
Because of great suffering, one regards minor suffering as pleasure; it is not true pleasure.
Furthermore, one regards old suffering as suffering and new suffering as pleasure.
It is like shifting a heavy burden from one shoulder to the other, taking the new weight as pleasure; it is not a truly constant pleasure.
Just as the nature of fire is heat, such that there is not even a moment when it is cold,
if this were true pleasure, there should be no instance of displeasure.
Someone might say:
“External phenomena are pleasant, yet their causal conditions are not necessarily pleasant; sometimes they are causes of pleasure, and sometimes they are causes of suffering.
If mental factors are associated with craving, at that time they are pleasant;
if they are associated with aversion, at that time they are painful.”
Associated with delusion, it is neither painful nor pleasant.
By inferring from this, one can know whether there is pleasure or no pleasure. He replied:
"No. Sensual desire should not be considered pleasure. Why is this?
If lust resides within, one should not seek out female forms externally; if one seeks out female forms externally, one should know that lust is suffering.
If lust were pleasure, one would not abandon it from time to time; if one abandons it, it cannot be pleasure.
Within great suffering, one takes minor suffering to be pleasure.
It is like a person who is destined for death; by sparing his life and receiving only a flogging, he considers this to be pleasure.
When the mind of desire is burning intensely, one takes desire to be pleasure; yet when one grows old and grows weary of desire, one realizes that desire is not pleasure.
If it were truly the characteristic of pleasure, one would not give rise to weariness toward it.
Thus, through various causes and conditions, the characteristic of sensual pleasure cannot be found in reality; when pleasure is lost, it becomes suffering.
The Buddha said:

"One should contemplate pleasant sensation as suffering; one should contemplate painful sensation as pleasure; and regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, which is like an arrow lodged in the body, one should contemplate it as impermanent through its arising and ceasing."
"This is called the application of mindfulness to feelings.
One should know that the mind experiences pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
What is the mind?
This mind is impermanent because it arises from causes and conditions.
It is subject to arising and ceasing without abiding; because it arises in a continuous succession of similar states, it is merely due to delusion that one regards it as a single entity.
That which was originally non-existent now exists, and that which has existed returns to non-existence;
therefore, it is impermanent. Contemplate and know that the mind is empty. Why is it empty?

Arising from causes and conditions: when there is the eye and visible forms that can be seen and recollected, and there is the desire to see such things, through their conjunction visual consciousness arises.
It is like the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*): when there is the sun, the gem, and dry grass or cow dung, through the conjunction of these various conditions, fire is produced.
If one investigates each [element] individually, fire cannot be found; it exists only when conditions combine.
Visual consciousness is likewise: it does not abide in the eye, nor does it abide in form, nor does it abide between the two. It has no place of abiding, yet it is not non-existent either.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"It is like an illusion, like a transformation.

When the present mind contemplates the past mind—whether it was painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—the minds are each distinct and each perishes. It is the same for the mind with desire and the mind without desire; they are each distinct and each perish. Contemplating the internal mind, contemplating the external mind, and contemplating both the internal and external minds are likewise so.
This is called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, one contemplates to whom the mind belongs;

one minutely observes the mind’s associated factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*)—such as perception, volition, and desire—as well as its dissociated factors (*citta-viprayukta-dharma*), scrutinizing their master, yet no such master can be found.

Why is this? Because they arise from causes and conditions, they are impermanent; because they are impermanent, they are suffering; because they are suffering, they lack self-mastery; because they lack self-mastery, they have no owner; and because they have no owner, they are empty.

Previously, one observed the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena individually and found them to be ungraspable; now, one further observes them collectively within the four foundations of mindfulness and finds that their primary essence is ungraspable, and even seeking it apart from these locations, it remains ungraspable.
If permanence cannot be found, impermanence likewise cannot be found;
if there were permanence, there would have to be constant suffering or constant bliss, and one could not forget them;
if there were a permanent self, there would be no sin of killing or harming, nor would there be nirvana.
If the body were the self, then when the impermanent body perishes, the self should also perish; there would be no future life, nor would there be sin or merit.

Thus, one observes universally that there is no master: all phenomena are empty and lack autonomy; they arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and they cease when causes and conditions disintegrate. This method of observing conditioned phenomena is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

If a practitioner attains the mindfulness of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) and becomes weary of the world as being empty of the nature of old age, sickness, and death—seeing that there is not even the slightest bit of permanence, bliss, self, or purity—they will think: "In these empty dharmas, what more is there for me to seek?"
One should enter and abide within the most excellent dharma of parinirvāṇa.

One should establish the power of diligence in order to attain profound *śamatha*. "Profound *śamatha*" is a term for the mind abiding in a single point; this term does not exist in this land [of Jambudvīpa].

At that time, having attained profound śamatha and abiding within the fourth dharma-smṛtyupasthāna, he contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena: they are all suffering and devoid of pleasure; this absence of pleasure is the truth, while everything else is false.

The causes of suffering—namely, the various afflictions such as craving and karma—are not produced from false notions such as those concerning a creator god (*īśvara*), time, or atoms; rather, they arise from these afflictions and karma. This suffering is indeed suffering.

At the time of entering nirvana, all things are extinguished; it is neither the realm of form nor the formless realm, nor the beginning of the world. While non-Buddhists claim that among all existing phenomena, form is the beginning of the world and call this "nirvana," [in reality] it is not so.

To claim that "because this has a beginning, it can transform and create the myriad things," which is termed "creation" (*zhaohua*), and so forth—such various false words can extinguish this suffering.

Right View and the other seven factors of the Eightfold Path are precisely the Way to Nirvana; they are not the ascetic practices of other heterodox paths, nor are they the various empty observances of precepts, empty meditative concentrations, or empty wisdoms.

Why is this? Within the Buddha-dharma, the three dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom, when practiced in combination, enable one to enter nirvana. It is like a person standing on level ground who, holding a fine bow and arrows, is able to shoot and kill an enemy; the combined practice of these three dharmas is likewise.

Precepts are the level ground; meditative concentration is the swift bow; wisdom is the sharp arrow. When these three things are fully perfected, one can slay the thieves of affliction. For this reason, those of external paths cannot attain nirvana.
At this time, the practitioner contemplates the four conditions of phenomena, observing conditions as one observes a target in archery.
One contemplates suffering in four ways:

it is impermanent because it arises from causes and conditions; it is suffering because the body and mind are afflicted; it is empty because not a single thing can be apprehended; and it is non-self because there is neither an agent nor an experiencer.
The contemplation of origination has four aspects:

it is "origination" because it is the conjunction of afflictions and outflowing karma; it is "cause" because it gives rise to similar fruits; it is "arising" because all conditioned phenomena are obtained therein; and it is "condition" because it constitutes the continuity of non-dissimilar fruits.
The contemplation of cessation has four aspects:

it is "closed" because it is covered by all afflictions; it is "extinguished" because the fire of afflictions is removed; it is "sublime" because it is the foremost among all phenomena; and it is "transcendent" because it has passed beyond the world.
The contemplation of the Path has four aspects:

it is the Path because it leads to Nirvana; it is Right because it is non-perverted; it is the Track because it is the place where all Noble Ones have gone; and it is Renunciation because it brings about liberation from worldly sorrow and affliction.
One who contemplates in this manner attains a dharma that resembles the untainted (anāsrava), which is called the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Why is it called "Heat"?
Because of constant and diligent application of energy, it is named the stage of Heat.

The fire of untainted wisdom burns the fuel of all afflictions; when the initial signs of this fire about to emerge appear, it is called the "Dharma of Heat" (*uṣmagata*). It is like drilling for fire: when smoke first issues from the drilling, it is called "heat. This is the initial sign of the path to Nirvāṇa.
Among the Buddha’s disciples there are two kinds of people:
first, those who predominantly delight in single-minded pursuit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); such persons follow the path with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Second, those who predominantly eliminate craving and attachment and delight in true wisdom (*prajñā*); such persons proceed directly toward *nirvāṇa* and enter into the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

One who possesses the sign of "warmth" (ūṣmagata) attains profound one-pointedness of mind; the mirror of the true dharma reaches the limit of the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu). The image within that mirror resembles a face, and because the limit of the realm is not the center, it is used as a metaphor.
At that time, the practitioner attains great peace and security, reflecting to himself:
"I shall certainly attain nirvāṇa, for I have seen this path.
It is like a person digging a well who, upon reaching moist mud, knows that he will obtain water before long.
It is like a person who strikes an enemy and, once the enemy has retreated and dispersed, knows for himself that he has achieved victory and feels secure in his mind;

or like a person who fears death and wishes to know whether he will live—first one must test him by striking his body with a staff; if hidden bruises appear and the pulse rises, one knows there is warmth, and thus he will certainly survive.

It is also like a person who hears the Dharma and, through contemplation, experiences joy and attachment; at that time, the mind becomes heated. Because the practitioner possesses such "heat" (*ūṣmagata*), it is called "the stage of heat," and it is also termed the "wholesome roots conducive to the attainment of Nirvana."

These roots of goodness consist of sixteen modes of activity regarding the Four Noble Truths; they take as their object the single wisdom within the six stages and serve as the foundation for all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. Because ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) can practice them, they find peace in the state of being distant from the untainted; thus they are called "ordinary people. This is according to the Sanskrit original. It is incorrect to refer to them first as "worldly persons" (*bālapṛthagjana*); this is what is termed the "Dharma of Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
As it progresses further upward, it is renamed the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdhan-dharma*), just as milk transforms into curd.

This person contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, thinking, "I shall attain liberation from suffering. Their mind cherishes this dharma, regarding it as the true dharma capable of eliminating all manner of afflictions, as well as old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, he reflected: "Who taught this Dharma?
It is the Buddha, the World-Honored One!
From this, he attained pure faith in the Jewel of the Buddha and experienced great joy and gladness.
If this Dharma did not exist, who would be able to obstruct all afflictions?
How could I obtain even a small measure of the light of true wisdom?
From this, I have attained pure faith and great joy within the treasure of the Dharma.
"If I were not to obtain the excellent companionship of the Buddha's disciples, how could I ever attain even a small measure of true wisdom and light?
From this, I have gained pure faith and great joy within the Sangha Jewel."

Within these Three Jewels, to attain single-minded purity and unite with true wisdom constitutes the "summit" root of goodness; it is also called the "Dharma of the Summit," and is further termed the root of goodness that can attain the portion of *nirvāṇa*.
As it is said in the *Pārāyaṇa Sūtra*:
"The Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha— Whoever possesses even a small measure of pure faith, This is called the 'Summit' wholesome root; You all should uphold it with a single mind."
What is meant by "little faith"?
It is little when directed toward Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats, and much when directed toward common folk;
furthermore, it is called "little" because it can be broken and lost.
As stated in the *Dharmapada*:
"The plantain dies when it bears fruit; the bamboo likewise perishes when it bears fruit!
The mule dies when it has offspring; the petty man dies when he receives nourishment."
"Because they have squandered what is not beneficial, the petty person gains a reputation;
having lost all that is pure and wholesome, they fall even from the 'Summit' stage.
Furthermore, because they have not yet severed the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*), immeasurable wisdom-mind, for this reason they are called "few."

Furthermore, when one enters the path to *nirvāṇa* with diligent effort and single-mindedness, one perceives the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the sixteen aspects of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*) even more clearly.
At that time, the mind does not shrink, regret, or retreat; it joyfully enters into receptivity (*kṣānti*). This is called the wholesome root of receptivity (*kṣānti-kuśalamūla*).
What is patience?
Following the contemplative practice of the Four Noble Truths is called patience.
This root of goodness is of three kinds:
There are three periods: superior, middling, and inferior.
What is called "patience" (kṣānti)?
It is when one contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; the mind remains patient and does not regress—this is called patience.

Furthermore, one contemplates that all worlds are entirely characterized by suffering and emptiness, devoid of any pleasure; that the causes of this suffering are the habitual tendencies of craving and other afflictions; and that the cessation of these tendencies through the wisdom of their conditions is called the "Supreme Dharma," beyond which there is nothing higher.
The Eightfold Noble Path can lead the practitioner to attain nirvāṇa, and there is nothing superior to it.
To have such faith without regret or doubt, and to accept this—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Within this, there is further patience (*kṣānti*): when various fetters (*saṃyojana*), various afflictions (*kleśa*), doubts, and regrets enter the mind, they cannot cause it to break. It is like a mountain of stone that various winds and waters cannot move or shake; therefore, it is called patience. For this reason, one earns the name of a "true wild man."
As the Buddha said in the *Dharmapada*:
"Whoever possesses the supreme right view in this world,
Even for ten million years, shall never fall into the evil realms."
"This is mundane right view; it is called the root of goodness that is patience (*kṣānti*).

This person greatly increases their progress, with a single mind deeply wearying of worldly activity, desiring to clearly understand the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, and realizing them as they proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. Such a state within a single moment of mind is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)."
At one time, they abide in four modes of practice:

impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; they contemplate the single truth because the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) takes it as its common object. Why is this?

Contemplating the five aggregates of clinging in the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, the mental patience that enters into wisdom therein, along with its associated mind and mental factors, is called the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

Physical action, vocal action, and formations dissociated from mind—all untainted dharmas of the present and future worlds—have this as their initial gateway; this is called the acceptance through faith in the dharma-patience regarding suffering and the patience regarding the dharma of the untainted dharmas.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering arises in succession.
The patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) severs the fetters and proclivities, while the dharma-knowledge of suffering provides realization.

It is like one person reaping and another person binding; it is also like using a sharp axe to cut bamboo, which falls immediately upon encountering the wind. Through the combined effort of patience and knowledge, this task is accomplished.

When the ten fetters are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana) pertaining to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), at that time, there is the acquisition of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), but untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet been acquired; rather, it is untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) that is acquired.

At that time, one wisdom—the conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna)—is accomplished; it is also accomplished in the future. In the second moment of mind, the dharma-wisdom (dharma-jñāna), the suffering-wisdom (duḥkha-jñāna), and the conventional wisdom are accomplished. Beyond the third and fourth moments of mind, four wisdoms are accomplished:
the suffering-wisdom, the dharma-wisdom, the subsequent wisdom (anvaya-jñāna), and the conventional wisdom.

Within the dharma-knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), exhaustion (*kṣaya*), and the path (*mārga*), each respective knowledge increases; for one who is free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is further accomplished and increased.

Through the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), eighteen fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned; these four moments of mind are capable of attaining the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Through the patience of conformity to the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmanirvedha*), one abandons the seven fetters bound to the desire realm;
through the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), one abandons the thirteen fetters bound to the realms of form and formlessness.

Through the patience regarding the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayadharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayadharma-jñāna*), one abandons the seven fetters bound to the desire realm;
through the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one abandons the twelve fetters bound to the form and formless realms.
The patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) sever the eight fetters bound to the desire realm;

the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) sever the fourteen fetters bound to the form and formless realms.

The path-knowledge and subsequent knowledge are called *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), the "son of the lower" and "son of the superior," who truly knows the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Among these sixteen moments of mind, those with sharp faculties during the first fifteen moments are called "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), while those with dull faculties are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
These two persons have not yet abandoned desire and are thus called those "progressing toward the first fruit" (*pratipannaka-prathama-phala*).
If they had not previously severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attain the sixteen moments of mind, they are called *srotāpanna*.
If they had previously severed six grades of fetters and attain the sixteen moments of mind, they are called *sakṛdāgāmin*—in the language of Qin, "Once-returner."
If one has previously severed the nine grades of fetters and attains the sixteen moments of mind, they are called an Anāgāmin (in the language of Qin, "Non-returner").
Because they have not yet abandoned desire but have severed eighty-eight fetters, they are called a Srotāpanna;
furthermore, because they have attained the acquisition of the wholesome roots of the untainted fruit, they are called a Srotāpanna.
Those of sharp faculties are called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); those of dull faculties are called "devoted through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*).

If the fetters of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been severed, they will undergo seven more births as remnants; if the three types of fetters of cultivation are severed, they are called "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṅkula*) and will undergo three more births.

The Noble Eightfold Path and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called "streams" because they flow toward Nirvana; since one flows along with them, it is named *srotāpanna*, and such a person is the first son of the Buddha's merit.
Having escaped from the evil realms, with the three fetters severed and the three poisons attenuated, one is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Furthermore, there are nine grades of fetters in the desire realm—namely, the superior-of-the-superior, superior-of-the-middle, superior-of-the-inferior, middle-of-the-superior, middle-of-the-middle, middle-of-the-inferior, inferior-of-the-superior, inferior-of-the-middle, and inferior-of-the-inferior—which are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If an ordinary person, having first severed the six types of fetters bound to the desire realm by means of the path with outflows, enters the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing the truths, they receive the name *sakṛdāgāmin*.
If there is an eightfold abandonment, upon entering the sixteenth moment of mind on the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), one type is called *srotāpattiphalapratipannaka-anāgāmī*.

If a disciple of the Buddha attains *srotāpanna*, having severed the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) alone, and seeks to attain *sakṛdāgāmin*, they contemplate the severance of the nine types of fetters bound to the desire realm and achieve the severance of six types;
this is called the eightfold severance of *sakṛdāgāmin*. This is called the first fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* directed toward *anāgāmin*.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has previously severed the nine kinds of fetters bound to the desire realm and enters the sixteenth moment of mind within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), they are called an *anāgāmin*.

If one who has attained the state of an *anāgāmin* proceeds further and severs the three kinds of fetters associated with cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), at the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), they are called an *anāgāmin*.

There are nine types of *anāgāmin*: the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* in this very life; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* after being born; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* through diligent effort; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* without diligent effort; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* by ascending higher; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; the *anāgāmin* who enters *nirvāṇa* upon reaching the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); and the *anāgāmin* who has realized the body (*kāyasākṣin*) and is proceeding toward arhatship.

Regarding the nine kinds of fetters of the form and formless realms, one destroys all these fetters through the ninth path of non-obstruction, the Vajra-samādhi; then, through the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and all roots of goodness—this is called the fruit of Arhatship.
There are nine types of arhats:

those subject to retrogression, those not subject to retrogression, those subject to death, those who maintain their state, those who abide in their state, those destined for final knowledge, those of unshakable nature, those liberated by wisdom, and those liberated both ways.
One who possesses dull wisdom and dull progress and regresses from the five kinds of dharmas is called one of the nature of regression (*parihāṇadharman*).
One who possesses sharp wisdom and sharp progress and does not regress from the five kinds of dharmas is called one of the nature of non-regression (*aparihāṇadharman*).
One with dull wisdom and dull diligence who, out of aversion toward contemplation, takes his own life—this is called the dharma of death.
One with dull wisdom but great diligence who protects his own life—this is called the dharma of preservation.
One of middling wisdom and middling progress who dwells in the state of neither increase nor decrease is said to abide in the Dharma.
One of limited benefit and wisdom who exerts diligent effort and is able to attain the indestructible liberation of mind is said to be one who will certainly know the Dharma.
One with sharp wisdom and great progress who first attains the liberation of mind that is indestructible is called one of "indestructible nature" (akopyadharman).
One who cannot enter the various dhyānas but has exhausted all outflows within the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) is called one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta).

Having attained the various dhyānas as well as the dhyāna of cessation (nirodha-dhyāna) and the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), this is called "liberation through both" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukti).
There is the Arhat who is constantly weary of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) and fully satisfied; no longer seeking further merit, he awaits the proper time to enter nirvāṇa.

There are Arhats who seek the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurables, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the ten totalities, the nine successive attainments, the six supernormal powers, the knowledge of aspiration, and the araṇa-samādhi (translated into Chinese as "non-contention").
"Āraṇya" means "without affairs," or it is said to mean "empty and tranquil.
The old [tradition] says that Subhūti always practices emptiness and tranquility; this is an error, for he actually practices the conduct of non-contention!

One who is free from contention protects sentient beings so as not to cause them to give rise to contention. Regarding the arising of contention within my own hearing, it was as when Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana stayed overnight in a pottery shed, which led Kokālika to give rise to contention. As for "transcending samādhi, perfuming dhyāna, and the three gates of liberation, as well as relinquishing and further relinquishing," the three gates of liberation are emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apraṇihita), and signlessness (animitta).

Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness are themselves the twelve gates of mindfulness for those who have turned away from attachment; by further cultivating sharp wisdom and diligent exertion, one enters into the merits of these various dhyānas—this is called attaining the dharma of non-retrogression and the dharma of indestructibility.
If a Buddha does not appear in the world, and there is neither the Buddha-dharma nor his disciples, at such a time a Pratyekabuddha who has abandoned desire appears.
There are three kinds of Pratyekabuddhas:
superior, middling, and inferior.
As for the inferior [type], they originally attain *srotāpanna* or *sakṛdāgāmin*.
This *srotāpanna*, after seven more births among humans, finds that at that time there is no Buddha-dharma and thus cannot become a disciple;
furthermore, they should not be born for an eighth time, at which point they become a *pratyekabuddha*.
If one were born in the two periods when the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* stages exist, at that time there would be no Buddha-dharma, and thus one could not become a disciple;
furthermore, one should not be born in the three periods [of the Buddha's absence], for at such times one becomes a *pratyekabuddha*.

There are those who vow to become pratyekabuddhas and plant the roots of goodness for a pratyekabuddha; at a time when the Buddha-dharma does not exist, their roots of goodness ripen, and they then grow weary of the world, leave the household life, and attain the Way, being called pratyekabuddhas—these are known as middle-level pratyekabuddhas.

There are those who seek the path of the Buddha but possess little power of wisdom or power of progress; they regress due to causes and conditions, as was the case with Śāriputra. At that time, no Buddha has appeared in the world, there is neither the Buddha-dharma nor disciples, yet their roots of goodness and practice have matured, and they become pratyekabuddhas. Whether their physical marks and signs are few or many, they grow weary of the world, leave the household life, and attain the Way; these are called superior pratyekabuddhas.
Among all dharmas, one who enters with shallow wisdom is called an Arhat;
one who enters to a medium degree is called a Pratyekabuddha;
and one who enters deeply is called a Buddha.
It is like seeing a tree from afar, where one cannot distinguish its branches;
as one draws slightly closer, one can distinguish the branches but not the flowers or leaves;
yet upon reaching the foot of the tree, one is able to discern and know the tree’s branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits in their entirety.
Śrāvakas are able to know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, that all dharmas are without a master, and that only nirvāṇa is truly peaceful and secure.
While śrāvakas can contemplate in this way, they are unable to analyze, penetrate, or understand it deeply;
pratyekabuddhas are able to analyze it slightly, yet they too cannot penetrate or understand it deeply.
The Buddha knows all phenomena through thorough analysis and complete mastery; he has entered deeply and understands profoundly.

It was as when the King of Vārāṇasī, during the heat of summer, sat upon a bed of the seven precious gems atop a high pavilion. He had his attendants grind ox-head sandalwood to anoint his body; these attendants wore many bracelets on their arms, and as they rubbed the king’s body, the sound of the bracelets filled his ears until he became greatly distressed by it.
He taught him step by step until he was liberated; as the bracelets became fewer, their sound grew faint until, with only a single bracelet remaining, it was silent and made no noise.
At that time, the king realized:
"The state, its ministers and subjects, the palace attendants, and the court ladies—all these many affairs and many afflictions are just like this!"
Immediately, becoming free from desire and dwelling in solitary contemplation, he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.

His hair and beard fell away naturally, and he was clothed in robes that appeared spontaneously; departing from the pavilion, he left the household life and entered the mountains by means of his own supernormal powers.
By such causes and conditions, one becomes a middle-grade pratyekabuddha.

If a practitioner seeks the Buddha-way and enters dhyāna, they should first bind the mind in single-minded recollection upon the birth-bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; they must not think of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor of mountains, trees, grasses, or wood, nor of any other material forms within heaven and earth, nor of any other dharmas—nothing at all should be thought of.
One should simply contemplate that the birth-bodies of all Buddhas abide in the void, like Mount Sumeru, the king of golden mountains, amidst the clear waters of the great ocean;
like a great blazing fire in the darkness of night;
or like a banner of the seven treasures within a great sacrificial offering.

The Buddha’s body is thus: it possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and constantly emits immeasurable, pure radiance. Within the blue hue of the characteristic of space, one should constantly contemplate the features of the Buddha’s body in this way; the practitioner will then attain the Samādhi of Seeing All Buddhas of the Ten Directions and Three Periods of Time Fully Present Before One’s Heart-Eye.

If the mind wanders to other objects, one should draw it back and cause mindfulness to abide upon the body of the Buddha; at that time, one will see three hundred thousand million, ten thousand million, and hundreds of millions of kinds of immeasurable Buddhas in the eastern direction.
In this way, in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—in whichever direction one directs one's thought—one sees all Buddhas.
It is like a person observing the stars at night; they see hundreds of thousands of immeasurable varieties of stars.
When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they cause the heavy karmic offenses of immeasurable kalpas to become light, and those that are light to be extinguished.

Having attained this samādhi, one should contemplate the various immeasurable merits of the Buddha: his all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), all-understanding (*sarvavijñapti*), all-seeing (*sarvadṛṣṭi*), and all virtues; his mastery over great loving-kindness and great compassion; and from his initial emergence from the shell of ignorance, his four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), ten powers (*daśabala*), and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*). These enable him to eliminate immeasurable suffering, rescue beings from the fear of old age and death, and bestow upon them the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha possesses such various and immeasurable merits; having formed this thought, he made this vow:
"When shall I attain the Buddha-body and the Buddha's merits, so sublime and majestic as these?"
He further made a great vow:
"I shall take all past merits and all present merits and dedicate them entirely toward seeking the Buddha-way, not for any other reward."
Again, he thought: "All sentient beings are truly pitiable.
The merits of the Buddhas' bodies are so sublime and majestic; why do sentient beings seek other karmic paths instead of seeking the Buddha?"
"It is like a blind son of a noble family who has fallen into a great, deep pit; starving and impoverished by suffering, he eats excrement and mud.
His father, feeling profound pity for him, seeks an expedient means to rescue him from the deep pit and feed him with choice delicacies."
The practitioner reflects:
"Such is the nectar of the merit of the Buddha’s two bodies, yet sentient beings fall into the deep pit of birth and death, consuming all manner of impurities."

With a heart of great compassion, I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings, enabling them to attain the Buddha-way and cross to the far shore of birth and death; I shall cause them all to be fully satiated with the flavor of the various meritorious dharmas of a Buddha, and I vow that they shall fully attain all the Buddha-dharmas.

Having heard that through recitation, retention, inquiry, and contemplative practice one attains the fruit, [the practitioner] establishes these as a ladder and makes a great essential vow, donning the armor of the three aspirations; thus they break the hosts of Māra externally and strike down the thieves of the fetters internally, entering directly forward without turning back.
"These three vows, when compared with immeasurable other vows, are all established for the sake of delivering sentient beings and attaining the Buddha-way.
Such mindfulness and such vows constitute the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
One who practices the bodhisattva path, if sexual desire is particularly excessive among the three poisons, should first contemplate their own body:

the bones, flesh, skin, tendons, veins, and flowing blood; the liver, lungs, intestines, stomach, excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva—the thirty-six impurities and the nine contemplations of the foul. They should focus their mind on internal observation without allowing external thoughts to arise;
should external thoughts concerning various conditions occur, they should restrain them and cause them to return [to the internal].
It is like a person holding a torch who enters a granary filled with various grains; they can discern and recognize every kind of bean, wheat, millet, and sorghum.
Furthermore, one contemplates the six components of the body:

that which is solid is the earth element, that which is moist is the water element, that which is hot is the fire element, that which moves is the wind element, that which is hollow is the space element, and that which cognizes is the consciousness element.
It is also like a butcher who divides an ox into six parts—the body, the head, and the four limbs—each situated in a different place.

The body has nine orifices from which impurities constantly flow; it is a leather bag filled with excrement. One should constantly maintain this contemplation so as not to allow external thoughts to arise;
if external thoughts of various conditions occur, one should restrain them and cause them to return [to the object of meditation].

If one attains single-mindedness and feels revulsion in one's mind, seeking to be free from this body and desiring its swift extinction so as to enter nirvana early, at that time one should give rise to great kindness and great compassion.
By means of great merit, one should rescue and deliver sentient beings, fulfilling the three previous vows:
"Because sentient beings do not understand impurity and thus give rise to various defilements of sin, I shall pull them out and place them upon the ground of ambrosia."
Furthermore, the sentient beings of the desire realm delight in and cling to impurity like dogs eating excrement; I shall deliver them and lead them to the path of purity.
Furthermore, I shall study and seek the true mark of all phenomena—which is neither permanent nor impermanent, and neither pure nor impure—so how could I cling to this impurity?

The wisdom that contemplates impurity arises from causes and conditions; as one who follows my Dharma, you should seek the true mark (dharmatā). Why then do you seek nirvana by merely feeling revulsion toward the impurities within the body?

One should be like a great elephant crossing a swift torrent, exhausting its source and bottom to attain the true characteristic of phenomena and enter Nirvana; how could one be like a monkey or a rabbit, terrified by the swift current, merely seeking to save its own body?

I shall now train myself according to the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas: practicing the contemplation of impurity to eliminate lustful desire, extensively transforming sentient beings to lead them away from the affliction of desire, yet not becoming weary or submerged by the contemplation of impurity itself.
Furthermore, once one has contemplated impurity and thus grown weary of birth and death, one should contemplate the gateway of purity by binding the mind to three locations:
the tip of the nose, the space between the eyebrows, and the forehead.
Within this [body], one should open an inch of skin, cleanly remove the flesh and blood, and fix the mind upon the white bones without allowing external thoughts;
should external thoughts arise regarding various conditions, one should restrain them and bring them back, focusing within the three conditions and constantly contending with the mind.
It is like two men wrestling: if the practitioner gains the upper hand, his mind will not follow [the distractions]; he restrains it and causes it to abide—this is called "one-pointedness of mind.

If, through the sense of revulsion, he gives rise to great compassion and takes pity on sentient beings who, for the sake of this empty skeleton, distance themselves from *nirvāṇa* and enter the three evil realms, he thinks: "I shall exert myself to perform all meritorious deeds and transform sentient beings, causing them to understand that the characteristics of the body are empty—that bones are covered by skin and are in reality a mass of impurities—and for the sake of sentient beings, I shall gradually analyze these various dharmic characteristics."
When there is a slight perception of purity, the mind gives rise to attachment;
when perceptions of impurity are numerous, the mind gives rise to weariness and aversion;
because there is the characteristic of the dharma of transcendence, the true dharma arises.

Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither purity nor impurity; there is neither closing nor emerging. To contemplate all phenomena as equal—indestructible and immovable—is called the true reality of all phenomena transcending the dharmas of the Arhats.

One who practices the bodhisattva path, if anger is particularly prevalent, should practice a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). One should contemplate the sentient beings of the eastern direction with a pure mind of loving-kindness—free from resentment and anger, vast and immeasurable—perceiving all sentient beings as if they were right before one's eyes.
The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
One should restrain the mind and practice loving-kindness, not allowing external thoughts to arise;
if external thoughts turn toward other conditions, one should collect them and bring them back.
Holding the mind and observing with the eyes, one sees all sentient beings clearly and distinctly, as if they were all before one's eyes.
If one attains single-mindedness, one should make this vow:
"By means of *nirvāṇa*, the truly pure Dharma, I shall deliver sentient beings and cause them to attain true happiness."
To practice the samādhi of loving-kindness with a mind such as this is the bodhisattva path.

Abiding in the samādhi of loving-kindness, one contemplates all dharmas as having a pure true nature that is indestructible and immovable, and vows to cause all sentient beings to attain the benefit of this dharma.

By means of this samādhi, one mindfully contemplates all sentient beings in the eastern direction with loving-kindness, causing them to attain the bliss of Buddhahood; it is the same for the ten directions!
The mind remains unshaken and undisturbed; this is called the Bodhisattva’s gate of the samādhi of loving-kindness.
Question: "Why not contemplate all sentient beings of the ten directions simultaneously? Answer:
"First, fix the mind on one direction; with a single-minded focus, it is easy to attain [compassion]. Thereafter, proceed sequentially until it pervades all directions. He asked:
"If a person has an enemy who constantly seeks to harm them, how can they practice loving-kindness (maitrī) with the desire to bring that person happiness?"
He replied: “Loving-kindness is a mental dharma that arises from the mind; it first proceeds toward those one holds dear.
As affection for them increases, it extends even to enemies, just as fire consumes wood, being capable of burning even when it is wet.”
Question: "At times sentient beings encounter various kinds of suffering, whether among humans or in the hells; even though the Bodhisattva is compassionate, how can they obtain happiness?"
He replied: "First, one takes the mark of pleasure from those who are joyful and causes those who are suffering to obtain such pleasure as they do.
It is like a defeated general who, losing his courage out of fear, regards even his enemies as heroes."
Question: "What are the beneficial virtues of practicing the samādhi of loving-kindness? Answer:
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"Having left the household life and departed from the secular world, I ought to practice a mind of loving-kindness.
He further contemplates, saying:
"Having partaken of the faithful offerings of others, one ought to practice for their benefit. As the Buddha said:
"To practice loving-kindness for even a brief moment is to follow the Buddha's teaching; this constitutes entering the Path and ensures that the offerings received are not in vain."
"Furthermore, although my body wears dyed robes, my mind should remain unstained; through the power of the samādhi of loving-kindness, it can keep me unstained.

Moreover, while the world destroys the Dharma, I am one who upholds the Dharma; amidst those who do not uphold the Dharma, I am one who upholds the Dharma. I shall be without affliction in accordance with the Dharma, by virtue of the power of the concentration of loving-kindness."
When a bodhisattva practices the path and approaches the gate of ambrosia, the various torments of feverish affliction are cooled by the refreshing bliss of compassion.
As the Buddha said:
"When a person is in the midst of extreme heat, they find joy upon entering a cool, refreshing pool."

Furthermore, one donning the armor of great compassion wards off the arrows of affliction; compassion serves as the medicinal elixir that neutralizes the poison of enmity and fetters. When afflictions scorch the mind, compassion can extinguish them;
compassion is the ladder of the Dharma for ascending the terrace of liberation.
Compassion is the vessel of the Dharma for crossing the ocean of birth and death; for those impoverished of the wealth of wholesome dharmas, compassion is the supreme jewel.
Proceeding toward Nirvana, loving-kindness serves as the provisions for the path;
loving-kindness serves as the swift steed, carrying one across into Nirvana;
loving-kindness serves as the valiant general, surmounting the three evil realms.
"One who is able to practice loving-kindness can subdue and eliminate all evils; the various devas and benevolent spirits will constantly follow and protect them. He asked:
"If a practitioner attains the samādhi of loving-kindness, how can they avoid losing it and instead cause it to increase?"

He replied: "To purify one's training in the precepts; to find joy in relying on wholesome faith; to train in the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); to possess single-minded wisdom; to delight in dwelling in seclusion and stillness; to always be heedful; to have few desires and be content; to act in accordance with the compassionate teachings; to moderate the body and eat sparingly; to diminish sleep, so that during the first and last watches of the night one does not cease contemplation; to reduce troublesome speech and maintain silence in stillness; and whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, to know the proper timing and measure so as not to lose the right degree, nor to cause excessive exhaustion or suffering, but to harmonize cold and warmth so as not to be disturbed—this is called 'benefiting through compassion.'"
"Furthermore, to bestow upon all people the joy of the Buddha-way and the joy of nirvana is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
The practitioner reflects:

'In the present and the future, great beings practice loving-kindness to benefit all; I too have been graced by this, which is my true blessing. I shall practice loving-kindness to fully repay their kindness.'"
Again, he further thought:

"The Great Virtuous One possesses a heart of compassion and takes pity on all beings, making this his joy; I too shall do likewise. By keeping those sentient beings in mind and causing them to attain the bliss of Buddhahood and the bliss of Nirvana, this shall be my way of repaying his kindness."
"Furthermore, Maitrībala, one can cause all beings to attain happiness of mind and freedom from the feverish afflictions of the body, obtaining the joy of coolness;
by maintaining the practice of the merit of loving-kindness and bringing peace to all, one repays their kindness."

Furthermore, loving-kindness possesses excellent benefits: it severs the dharma of ill-will, opens the gate of reputation, serves as a fertile field for donors, acts as the cause for rebirth in the Brahma heavens, establishes one in a state free from desire, and eliminates adversaries as well as the roots of strife.

Praised by all Buddhas and revered by the wise, one who is able to uphold the pure precepts gives rise to the light of wisdom; such a person can hear the benefits of the Dharma—the very cream of merit—and being resolutely a good person, they exert the vigor of renunciation to extinguish all evils.

Abuse and unwholesome conduct are subdued by the retribution of loving-kindness; it gathers joy and gives rise to the dharma of diligence. It is the root cause of wealth and nobility, the establishment of the treasury of wisdom, and the storehouse of sincerity and faith. It comprises all gates of wholesome dharmas, leads to the dharma of renown and praise, and is the foundation of reverence—the Buddha’s path of true correctness.
"If a person harbors ill will toward others, they will return to receive its calamity themselves.
There are five kinds of evil speech:
untimely speech, untruthful speech, unbeneficial speech, unkind speech, and harsh speech."

These five evil words cannot shake him, nor can any poison or harm injure him; it is like a small fire that cannot heat the great ocean. [Below this, there should appear the account of King Udayana holding five hundred hair-arrows.]
As stated in the *Vīra-sūtra* in the *avadāna* of King Udayana, he had two queens:
the first was named Anupamā, and the second was named Śyāmavatī.
The peerless Śamīpati slandered [the Buddha].
Śamīpati had five hundred upright men, whom the king intended to shoot and kill one by one with five hundred arrows.
Śyāmavatī said to the attendants, "Stand behind me.
At that time, Śyāmavatī entered the samādhi of loving-kindness; when the king drew his bow and shot at her, the arrow fell at her feet.
The second arrow returned toward the king’s feet.
The king was greatly terrified and again wished to release an arrow.
Śamīpāti said to the king:
"Stop, stop! It is for the sake of the righteousness between husband and wife that I speak thus; had you released this arrow, it would have pierced right through your heart.
At that time, the King was struck with fear; he cast aside his bow, abandoned his shooting, and asked:
"What skill do you possess?
He replied, "I have no extraordinary skill."
"I am a disciple of the Buddha, for I have entered the samādhi of loving-kindness!
"This samādhi of loving-kindness, briefly stated, has three kinds of objects:
the object of sentient beings (sattvālambana), the object of phenomena (dharmālambana), and the objectless (anālambana)."
Those who have not yet attained the Path are called "those conditioned by sentient beings" (sattvālambana).
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are called "those conditioned by phenomena" (dharmālambana).
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called "those without conditions" (anālambana); therefore, the gate of the Samādhi of Loving-kindness is explained in brief.
