For one practicing the bodhisattva path, if delusion (*moha*) predominates among the three poisons, they should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination to destroy two kinds of delusion:
internally destroying delusion regarding the body, and externally destroying delusion regarding sentient beings.
He reflected and thought:

"I and all sentient beings are together in distress and calamity—constantly born, constantly aging, constantly ill, constantly dying, constantly perishing, and constantly emerging. Sentient beings are pitiable; they do not know the way out. From what can they be liberated?"

He reflected single-mindedly: "Birth, old age, sickness, and death arise from causes and conditions. What, then, are the causes and conditions from which they arise? Reflecting single-mindedly, he realized: birth arises conditioned by existence;

existence arises conditioned by grasping; grasping arises conditioned by craving; craving arises conditioned by feeling; feeling arises conditioned by contact; contact arises conditioned by the six sense bases; the six sense bases arise conditioned by name-and-form; name-and-form arises conditioned by consciousness; consciousness arises conditioned by mental formations; and mental formations arise conditioned by ignorance.
Thus he further reflected: "By what causes and conditions do birth, old age, and death cease? With single-minded reflection, he realized: through the cessation of birth, old age and death cease;

through the cessation of existence (*bhava*), birth ceases; through the cessation of grasping (*upādāna*), existence ceases; through the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping ceases; through the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*), craving ceases; through the cessation of contact (*sparśa*), feeling ceases; through the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact ceases; through the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases cease; through the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form ceases; through the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness ceases; and through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations cease.
Within these twelve divisions, what is the division of ignorance?
It is not knowing the past, not knowing the future, not knowing both the past and the future; not knowing the internal, not knowing the external, not knowing both the internal and the external;
and not knowing the Buddha, not knowing the Dharma, and not knowing the Saṅgha. Not knowing...
Not knowing suffering, not knowing its origin, not knowing its cessation, and not knowing the path;
not knowing karma, not knowing its fruit, and not knowing the fruit of karma; not knowing causes, not knowing conditions, and not knowing causes and conditions;
not knowing transgression, not knowing merit, and not knowing both transgression and merit; not knowing what is wholesome, and not knowing what is unwholesome...
They do not know what is wholesome; they do not know what is unwholesome; they do not know which dharmas are faulty and which are faultless;
they do not know which dharmas should be approached and which should be avoided; they do not know which dharmas are with outflows and which are without outflows;
they do not know which dharmas are mundane and which are supramundane; they do not know the transcendence [of these].
They do not know the dharma of passing away; they do not know future dharmas, nor do they know present dharmas.

They do not know dark dharmas, nor do they know bright dharmas. They do not know the dharma of discerning causes and conditions, nor do they know the dharma of the six contacts, nor do they know the dharma of actual realization.
Such various forms of non-knowing, lack of wisdom, lack of vision, darkness, and ignorance are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). What are called volitional formations?
There are three kinds of formations:
bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations.
What are bodily formations?
Inhalation and exhalation are bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*). Why is this so?
Because these phenomena belong to the body, they are therefore called bodily formations.
What are verbal formations?

There is initial application (vitarka) and sustained application (vicāra); having produced this initial and sustained application, one then speaks with the voice. If there were no initial and sustained application, there would be no speech; these are called verbal formations.
What are the mental formations?

"Pain" refers to the three kinds of sensation to which people in the world are attached; "pain" should properly be called "feeling. Through feeling, one experiences pleasure and pain according to the realm. Since these do not exist in the higher realms, it is appropriate to say that the afflictions from which the renunciant departs are feeling and perception.
Painful perception is a mental dharma; because it is bound to the mind, it is called a mental formation (*manosaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there are formations bound to the desire realm, formations bound to the form realm, and formations bound to the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are wholesome courses of action, unwholesome courses of action, and immovable courses of action.
What are wholesome courses of action?
They are all wholesome courses of action in the desire realm, as well as those in the first three stages of the form realm.
What are unwholesome formations?
They are all unwholesome phenomena (*dharma*).
What are immovable formations?
The contaminated wholesome karma of the fourth dhyāna, as well as the contaminated wholesome karma of the formless attainments—
these are called formations.
Formations are the condition for consciousness.
What is called consciousness?
The six elements of consciousness:
from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; these are called the six consciousnesses.
With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.
What is "name"? The four formless aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are called "name."
What is form? All forms consisting of the four great elements and derived form—this is called form.
What are the four great elements?
Earth, water, fire, and wind. What is earth?

That which has the characteristic of solidity and heaviness is earth; that which has the characteristic of moisture is water; that which has the characteristic of heat is fire; that which has the characteristic of lightness and motion is wind.
The remaining forms that are visible, whether they possess resistance or lack resistance, are called derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The conjunction of name and form is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
With name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise.
What are the six sense bases?
The six internal sense bases:
from the internal sense base of the eye up to the internal sense base of the mind; these are called the six sense bases.
With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact.
What is contact? It consists of the six classes of the contact element:
From eye-contact up to mind-contact. What is eye-contact?
When the eye conditions visible forms, eye-consciousness arises; the coming together of these three factors is called eye-contact. It is the same for all [contacts] up to mind-contact.
With contact as condition, there is feeling.
What is feeling? There are three kinds of feeling: [pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant].
There are pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
What is a pleasant feeling? It is the underlying tendency of craving.
What is the painful feeling?
It is the underlying tendency toward aversion. What is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
The latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). Furthermore, a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) arises from pleasure, abides in pleasure, and ceases with suffering;
a painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) arises from suffering, abides in suffering, and ceases with pleasure.
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not know suffering nor does one know pleasure.
With feeling as condition, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What is craving?
From eye-contact with forms arises craving, and so on, up to mind-contact with mental phenomena arising craving.
With craving as condition, there is clinging (*upādāna*). What is clinging?
The grasping for sensual pleasures, the grasping for views, the grasping for precepts and observances, and the grasping for the doctrine of self.
With grasping as condition, there is existence. What is existence?
There are three kinds of existence:
existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm.
These extend downward from the great Avīci hell.

From the lowest level up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), this is called "existence in the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) along with the karma that can produce it.
What is "existence in the form realm" (*rūpadhātu-bhava*)? From the Brahma-world below up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven above, this is called "existence in the form realm."
What is existence in the formless realm?
From the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called existence in the formless realm.
It arises from causes and conditions.

What is birth? The emergence of various sentient beings in various places, wherein there is the acquisition of the aggregates (skandhas), the bases (āyatanas), the elements (dhātus), and life—this is called birth.
Birth is the condition for old age and death.
What is old age?

The falling out of teeth, the whitening of hair, the abundance of wrinkles, the maturation of the faculties, the decay of the faculties, the choking of breath, the stooping of the body, walking with the aid of a staff, and the decrepitude of the physical aggregate—this is called old age.
What is death? When all sentient beings everywhere undergo withdrawal, falling away, decline, cessation, severance, and die—losing their life-force and reaching its end—this is called death.
Because aging occurs first and death follows later, it is called "aging-and-death.

Within these twelve links of dependent origination, all worlds do not arise from the extreme of causelessness, nor from the extreme of a creator god, nor from the extreme of a human being, nor from the extreme of various other false conditions.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, binding the mind so that it does not waver and preventing external thoughts;
he gathers back all external thoughts regarding various conditions and causes them to return.
He contemplates the twelve factors of birth within the three periods of time:
Past lives, present lives, and future lives.
If a bodhisattva attains stability of mind, they should contemplate that the twelve links of existence are empty and devoid of a master.
Ignorance does not know that formations arise from it; formations do not know that they exist because of ignorance; rather, formations arise solely due to the condition of ignorance.

Just as the seeds of grasses and trees produce sprouts from their seeds, yet the seed does not know, "I am producing the sprout," nor does the sprout know, "I have emerged from the seed"—even so it is with everything up to old age and death!

Within these twelve divisions [of the scriptures], one should observe and know each one to be without a master and without a self; they are like external grasses and trees that have no owner, yet people falsely perceive a "self" due to inverted views.
Question: "If there is no self, no master, and no agent, how can one speak of going and coming, or of dying here and being born there? Answer:

"Although there is no self, with the six sense faculties acting as causes and the six sense objects acting as conditions, the six consciousnesses arise within. Because these three factors combine, contact arises; one then perceives and knows various karmas, and through this, there is coming and going. From this, speech arises, and thus there is birth and death."
For example, as fire emerges from a sun-crystal through the conjunction of the sun and dried cow dung by means of appropriate conditions, so it is with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*):

because of these five aggregates, the five aggregates of a future life arise. It is not that these present five aggregates travel to the future life, nor is it that one obtains the five aggregates of the future life apart from these present five aggregates; the five aggregates simply emerge from causes and conditions.

For example, when a sprout emerges from a grain seed, that seed is not the sprout, nor does it arise from another sprout; they are neither different nor identical. It is the same for obtaining a body in a future life!

For example, when a tree has not yet developed its trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, it becomes fully endowed with flowers and leaves once the conditions of the seasons are met; the retribution for wholesome and unwholesome deeds is likewise so.
Because the seed perishes, it is neither permanent nor unitary;
because the sprout, stem, leaves, and so forth arise, it is neither annihilated nor different.
The continuity of death and birth is likewise thus.
The practitioner contemplates that phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, arising and ceasing of their own accord.

He knows that they exist due to craving and other such causes, and he knows that their cessation through the extinction of those causes is "exhaustion" (nirodha); he knows that this knowledge of exhaustion is the "path" (mārga).
To know the twelvefold [scriptures] by means of the four kinds of knowledge is the path of right view.
Sentient beings are deceived by their attachments, like a person who possesses a priceless jewel but fails to distinguish its authenticity, thereby being cheated by others.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a heart of great compassion, vowing: "I shall become a Buddha and transform those sentient beings with the true and correct Dharma, causing them to see the Right Path.
He asked: "As it is said in the *Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā*:"
"All dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing; they are empty and non-existent, having a single mark which is marklessness—this is called right view.
Why, then, do you say that the contemplation of impermanence and so forth is called right view?
He replied: "If the Mahāyāna teaches that 'all dharmas are empty and signless,' why do you say that impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth are unreal?"
If you claim that emptiness—which is neither arising nor ceasing—is the true nature (*dharmatā*), then you should not say it is "signless" (*animitta*).
Your statement is internally inconsistent from beginning to end.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught the four inversions; there is also a logical basis for the inversion of perceiving permanence within impermanence, for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are impermanent.
Why is this? Because it arises from causes and conditions.
Since the causes are impermanent and the conditions are impermanent, how could the fruit produced thereby be permanent?
That which was previously non-existent now exists, and having existed, it then ceases to be.

All sentient beings perceive impermanence: internally there is aging, sickness, and death; externally they see the withering and falling away of all things. How can you say that impermanence is not real?
He asked: "I do not say that permanence is real and impermanence is unreal; I say that both permanence and impermanence are unreal."
Why is this? The Buddha said:
"Within emptiness, both permanence and impermanence are unattainable; if one clings to these two things, both are inversions."
He replied: "What you say does not accord with the Dharma. Why is this?"
If you say there are no dharmas, why do you further say that both are inverted?
That all things are empty and non-existent is the reality and is not inverted.

If I were to destroy the attachment to permanence by means of impermanence, then my dharma would be subject to destruction and would not be real; since I possess the inversion of permanence, I observe impermanence in order to destroy it.

Why is this? The power of impermanence can destroy that which is permanent, just as poison can neutralize other poisons, or as medicine eliminates disease; yet when the disease is removed, the medicine also departs. One should know that the medicine is excellent precisely because it is able to eliminate the disease.
If the previous medicine does not depart, the subsequent medicine becomes a disease; this is also like that!
If one is attached to impermanent phenomena, they ought to be destroyed because they are unreal.
Since I do not accept impermanent phenomena, how could they be destroyed?
The Buddha said:
"Regarding suffering among the Four Noble Truths, it is called 'actual suffering. Who could make it pleasant?
Regarding the cause of suffering, it is the actual cause. Who could make it not a cause?"
The exhaustion of suffering is true exhaustion; who could cause it not to be exhausted?
The Path to Exhaustion is the true Path; who could cause it not to be the Path?
Even if one could make the sun cold, the moon hot, or the wind motionless, these Four Noble Truths can never be altered or overturned.
"You do not understand the Mahāyāna, but merely cling to words and sounds.
Within the Mahāyāna, the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is such that this true mark cannot be destroyed, nor is there any agent."
If it can be destroyed or created, this is not the Mahāyāna.
It is like the new moon: on the first and second days, when it first arises, its appearance is extremely subtle; yet a person with clear vision can see it and point it out to those who cannot.
This person does not see the moon, but looks only at its finger and is thus deluded regarding the moon.
A wise person says to him: "Fool!"
"Why do you look only at my finger?
The finger is merely a condition for the moon; the finger is not that moon.
You, too, are just like this!
"Words and sounds are not the true nature; they merely use provisional language to express the ultimate reality.
If you further cling to words and sounds, you will remain ignorant of the true nature.
If one attains such correct knowledge and vision, one contemplates the twelve links [of dependent origination] as being synthesized into two parts: cause and effect.

The twelve factors at the time of the fruit constitute the Truth of Suffering; the twelve factors at the time of the cause constitute the Truth of Origination; the cessation of the cause constitutes the Truth of Cessation; and the vision of the exhaustion of cause and effect constitutes the Truth of the Path.
The four kinds of contemplation on the fruit:
impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The four kinds of contemplation on the cause:
Aggregation, cause, condition, and arising.
Question: "There are four kinds of fruits, yet only the first is named the Truth of Suffering; do the others lack the designation of 'truth'?"

He replied: "If one says that the truth of impermanence is doubted, then the truth of suffering is also doubted, and the truth of non-self is also doubted; these constitute the same kind of difficulty.
Furthermore, if one says there is no fault in the truth of impermanence, then there is likewise no fault in the truths of emptiness and non-self."
If the truths of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are taught as being weighty, for this reason one [truth] is spoken of among the four.
Question: "What distinct characteristic does suffering have that it alone is given a name among the three?"
He replied: "Suffering is that which all sentient beings loathe and fear; impermanence is not so.
While some people, oppressed by suffering, may seek impermanence, there is no one who seeks suffering."

Question: "Are there not people who wish to seize a blade to commit suicide, or who enter among bandits despite the pain of acupuncture, moxibustion, and bitter medicines—such various acts as these being sought for the sake of suffering?"
He replied: "It is not that they desire to obtain suffering, but rather that they wish to preserve great happiness; it is out of fear of suffering that they choose death.

Suffering is the foremost affliction, and happiness is the foremost benefit. For this reason, by departing from actual suffering one attains true happiness; therefore, the Buddha designated only the aspect of the fruit as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and not as the truths of impermanence, emptiness, or non-self."
To have clear and thorough wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths, without doubt or regret, is called Right View.
To contemplate these matters and further augment them in various ways is called Right Resolve.

Excluding those [factors] subsumed under wrong livelihood that comprise the four kinds of wrong speech, one is separated from the remaining four kinds of wrong speech; this comprises the four kinds of right speech. Excluding those [factors] subsumed under wrong livelihood that comprise the three kinds of bodily action, one is separated from the remaining three kinds of wrong action; this is called right action.
To be free from other various forms of wrong livelihood is called right livelihood.
To exert diligence when contemplating in this way is right effort.
For the mind not to be distracted from this matter is called right mindfulness.
To remain unmoved while contemplating this matter is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Right awakening is like a king, with these seven matters following in attendance; this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
To maintain single-mindedness and firm faith in this matter without wavering is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To seek the Way with single-minded diligence is called the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*).
To maintain mindfulness with a single mind without forgetting is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
For the mind to abide in one place without wandering or scattering is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
The discernment and analytical reflection upon the awakening to impermanence and so forth is called the faculty of wisdom.
This is called "increasing and attaining power," and it is called the five powers (*pañca-balāni*). Question:

Question: “Since wisdom, mindfulness, concentration, and so forth are all explained within the Eightfold Noble Path, why are they mentioned again among the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*)? Answer:
“When one enters into practice and initially attains minor benefits, at that time they are called faculties.”
When these five factors increase and gain power, they are then designated as "powers.
Upon first entering the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) which is free from outflows (anāsrava), these qualities are called the Eightfold Noble Path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).
When entering the path of contemplation, it is called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

At the initial entry into the path, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena with constant single-minded mindfulness; this is called the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
Thus, attaining the four kinds of diligent application through the flavor of wholesome dharmas is called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Thus, desire, vigor, concentration, and wisdom are the initial gates; diligently applying vigor to seek mastery according to one's wish is called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Although they are named the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, and so forth, each receives its respective name by encompassing the objects of focus and the stages of practice—whether initial or final, few or many—during the course of their cultivation.
For example, within each of the four great elements (mahābhūta), there are further instances of the four great elements; however, they receive their names based on what predominates.
If the earth element (pṛthivī-dhātu) is predominant while the water, fire, and wind elements are scarce, it is designated as the "earth great element" (pṛthivī-mahābhūta).
Water, fire, and wind are also like this!

Likewise, within each of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, there are various sub-factors; for example, within the four foundations of mindfulness, there are the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, and so forth.

Observing in this way the twelve links [of dependent origination], the practice of the four truths, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, his mind becomes peaceful and blissful.
Furthermore, using this Dharma to deliver sentient beings, he single-mindedly vows and strives with diligence to seek Buddhahood.
At that time, he reflects and contemplates within his mind:
"I clearly observe and know this Path; I should not realize its fruit."
There are two powers by virtue of which he has not yet entered nirvana:
first, his great compassion that does not abandon sentient beings; second, his profound realization of the true mark of all phenomena.
All mental states and their associated factors arise from causes and conditions; how could I now follow this unreality?
I should reflect for myself, desiring to enter deep contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, so as to know what kind of phenomena these causes and conditions are.
Furthermore, one further contemplates these four kinds of conditions:
the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The five causes constitute the causal condition. With the exception of the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat in the past or present, all other past and present minds and mental factors constitute the immediate condition.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) take all phenomena as their objects.
Furthermore, he reflects to himself:
"If a phenomenon already exists within its causal conditions, then one should not say that this phenomenon is produced by those causal conditions."
If it does not exist, one should not say that it arises from causes and conditions;
nor should that which is half-existent arise from causes and conditions.
How, then, can there be causes and conditions?
If a dharma has not yet arisen, or if past mental states and their concomitants have already perished, how can they function as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Furthermore, if in the Buddha’s teaching the sublime Dharma—nirvana without conditions—is itself without conditions, how can it serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
If all phenomena truly lack intrinsic nature, then no phenomenon can be apprehended;
if a result arises from causes and conditions such that "because of this, that exists," then that statement is not tenable.
Whether the causes and conditions exist individually or in combination as one, that result cannot be found; how, then, could a result emerge from the side of causes and conditions?
Because the effect does not exist within the causes and conditions.
If the effect were to emerge while previously being non-existent within the causes and conditions, why would it not emerge from that which is not a cause or condition?
For in both cases, [the effect] is equally absent.

If a fruit belongs to causes and conditions and arises from the side of causes and conditions, then those causes and conditions are not independent as they belong to other causes and conditions; thus, that fruit belongs to other causes and conditions.
Why are they not independent?

Since causes and conditions can produce an effect, that effect does not exist apart from causes and conditions, nor does it exist apart from what are not causes and conditions; if it were so, it would not be an effect.
Because the effect does not exist, both conditions and non-conditions likewise do not exist!
Question: “The Buddha taught the twelve links of dependent origination, wherein ignorance conditions volitional formations; how can you say there is no cause and effect? Answer:
"You have already been answered; you should not raise further objections, for if you do, I shall answer again.

The Buddha said that with the eye as cause and forms as condition, there arises from the side of delusion (*moha*) false recollection. Delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*). Within this, upon what does this ignorance depend and abide?"
Is it by depending on the eye?
Or within form? Or within consciousness?
It should not abide by depending on the eye.
If it were to abide dependent on the eye, it should not depend on form and would be constantly deluded.
If it were to abide dependent on form, it should not depend on the eye.
This would then be external delusion; how could it concern my affairs?
If one relies on the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness is formless, non-obstructive, intangible, partless, and without location.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise; how could it abide?

Therefore, ignorance is neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two; it does not come from a previous life, nor does it abide in a future life; it does not come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below. It has no real substance; such is the nature of ignorance.
When the nature of ignorance is fully understood, it is transformed into clarity; if one investigates each instance, delusion cannot be found.
How can there be "ignorance as a condition for volitional formations"?
It is like space, which is neither born nor extinguished, neither existent nor exhausted, and whose fundamental nature is pure.

Ignorance is also like this: it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor exhausted; its intrinsic nature is pure, and the same applies even to birth as the condition for old age and death.

When a bodhisattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in this way, they know that sentient beings are delusively bound within suffering and affliction, and are thus easy to deliver.
If all phenomena possessed a real mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), they would be difficult to deliver; by reflecting in this manner, one destroys ignorance.

If a bodhisattva’s mind is characterized by many discursive thoughts, they should constantly practice mindfulness of ānāpāna, counting from one up to ten as the breath enters and exits, ensuring that with each instance the mind does not wander or scatter.
From this gate, the bodhisattva attains single-mindedness and eliminates the five hindrances that lead to desire.
When the bodhisattva perceives the Path, they should practice three kinds of patience:
patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*), patience in accordance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*), and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
What is the patience of birth?

When all sentient beings revile, strike, or kill one, or engage in various other evil deeds, the mind remains unmoved, without anger or resentment; not only does one endure this, but one further responds with compassion and loving-kindness, wishing that these sentient beings may seek all that is good and attain it all, never abandoning them in thought.
At that time, he gradually attains the realization of the true nature of all phenomena, like a fragrance permeating its substrate.

It is like a compassionate mother who loves her infant; she nourishes and raises it with milk, not regarding various impurities as foul, but instead redoubling her pity and concern, desiring only for the child to attain happiness.
The practitioner is likewise: though all sentient beings commit various evils and perform both pure and impure deeds, their mind does not increase in malice, nor does it retreat or waver.

Furthermore, [they think], "I alone must deliver the immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions, causing them all to attain the Buddha-way. Within this patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*), they fix their single-minded attention, remaining patient, non-retrogressive, unrepentant, undaunted, untiring, fearless, and undismayed.
To prevent external thoughts through three kinds of reflection, and to gather back those external thoughts toward their conditions, is called the patience of endurance (*utpattikṣānti*).
What is the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikadharmakṣānti*)?

Once the Bodhisattva has attained the patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*), his merit is immeasurable; yet, knowing that the karmic rewards of this merit are impermanent, he then becomes weary of impermanence and seeks for himself eternal bliss, while also seeking the eternally abiding Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

One seeks the true characteristic of all dharmas: dharmas that are material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, and those that are superior, middling, or inferior.
What is the true nature?
It is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither blissful nor non-blissful, neither empty nor non-empty, and neither possessing a self nor being selfless.
Why is it not permanent? Because it arises from causes and conditions;
because what was previously non-existent now exists, and what has already existed returns to non-existence; therefore, it is not permanent.
Why is it not impermanent?
Because karmic retribution is never lost, because one experiences external objects, and because causes and conditions continue to increase, it is not impermanent.
Why is it not pleasant?
Because one conceives the notion of pleasure within new suffering, because all things are impermanent by nature, and because it arises conditioned by desire, it is therefore not pleasure.
Why is it not non-pleasure?
Because pleasure involves sensation, because it gives rise to desire and defilement, and because one seeks pleasure without sparing one's own body, it is not non-pleasure.

Why is it not empty? Because the internal and external sense bases each experience their objects with distinct clarity; because there exist the retributions of sin and merit; and because all sentient beings have faith [in these things], it is therefore not empty.
Why is it not non-empty?

Because the combination and so forth are real; because they cannot be found when sought through conceptual analysis; and because the power of the mind undergoes transformation—for these reasons, it is not non-empty.
Why is it that there is no self?
Because it lacks sovereignty, because the seventh consciousness-element cannot be apprehended, and because the characteristics of a self cannot be apprehended; therefore, there is no self.
Why is it not that there is no self?
Because there is a future life; because one attains liberation; and because the thought "I" arises individually without reckoning any other locus—therefore, it is not that there is no self.

Thus, it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither non-arising nor non-ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent, neither receiving nor clinging; all verbal expressions are extinguished and the sphere of mental activity is severed. Like the nature of nirvāṇa, this is the true reality of dharmas.

Within this Dharma, one’s faith is pure, free from stagnation and unimpeded; with gentle knowledge, gentle faith, and gentle diligence, this is called the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
What is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*)?

Within the aforementioned dharmas of true reality (*tathatā*), when wisdom, faith, and diligence increase so that the faculties become sharp, this is called the "patience regarding non-arising dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

It is like the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*) in the Śrāvaka teachings: through the increase of wisdom, faith, and vigor, one attains the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*). Because one endures (*kṣamate*) nirvāṇa and endures untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), it is called "patience."
Because one newly attains and newly perceives [the truth], it is called "patience" (kṣānti).
The same applies to the patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti).

A time-liberated arhat who has not yet attained the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) advances toward greater benefit and transforms into an untimely liberated arhat (asamayavimukta), thereby attaining the knowledge of non-arising.

The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is also like this: having not yet attained the fruit of a bodhisattva, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas and thereby attains the fruit of the true practice of a bodhisattva; this is called the fruit of the bodhisattva path.
At that time, they attain the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, develop great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings, and enter the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Then, the Buddhas grant them their names; they are born within the Buddha-fields, are held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas, and their heavy sins are lightened—those that are light being extinguished—and the three evil realms are severed. They are constantly reborn among devas and humans, and are called "non-retrogressive."

Upon reaching the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), at the very end, the physical body is entirely absorbed into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). One is then able to manifest various transformations to deliver all sentient beings, fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) to make offerings to all Buddhas, purify Buddha-lands, and teach sentient beings. Establishing oneself within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one brings merit to full completion and successively attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This constitutes the initial gateway among the dhyāna-methods of the bodhisattvas.
When the practitioner seeks the Way with a concentrated mind, they should always observe the timing and skillful means;
if one fails to find the right time and lacks skillful means, this should be regarded as a loss rather than a gain.
As one milks a cow before the calf has been born, milk cannot be obtained because it is the wrong time;
if one milks a cow after the calf has already been born, milk cannot be obtained because of a lack of wisdom.
As one who drills damp wood seeking fire, fire cannot be obtained because it is the wrong time;
as one who breaks dry wood seeking fire, fire cannot be obtained because of a lack of wisdom.
Knowing the place, the time, and measuring one's own conduct; observing the strength of the mind’s skillful means;
whether it is appropriate to apply diligence or not; and whether the signs of the Path are favorable or unfavorable at that time.
If the mind is agitated, one should not exert force; likewise, through such forceful effort, one does not attain concentration.
It is like a great fire with abundant fuel that refuses to be extinguished when a strong wind blows upon it.
If one can discipline the mind through meditative concentration, then through such movement and stillness, the mind attains stability;
just as a great fire blown by a mighty wind is extinguished without exception when doused by a torrent of water.
If one’s mind is soft and further indolent, such a person will sink into weariness and fail to practice;
like a fire with little fuel and no flame, it will extinguish of its own accord when not fanned by the wind.
If one possesses a mind of diligent and courageous effort, thus becoming increasingly robust, one attains the Way swiftly;
just as a small fire, when much fuel is added and fanned by the wind, blazes ever more fiercely without ceasing.
If one practices equanimity while failing to restrain or discipline the mind, and further abandons it, one loses the protection of the Dharma;
just as a patient must be carefully nurtured, if they are abandoned, they will not survive.
If one possesses equanimity and a rightly balanced mind, one should practice diligently at this time to swiftly attain the Way;
it is like a person riding a well-trained elephant, reaching their destination as they wish without stumbling or obstruction.
If one’s mind is agitated by excessive lust and craving, at such a time one should not practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the like;
for a lustful person practicing loving-kindness only increases their delusion and distress, like a person with a cold disease taking cold medicine.
The lustful person’s mind is distracted; by contemplating impurity, they contemplate with clarity and the mind attains concentration.
Because practicing the Dharma in such a corresponding manner, it is like a person with a cold ailment taking hot medicine.
If one’s mind is filled with much anger and agitation, at such a time one should not contemplate impurity;
for an angry person contemplating foulness only increases their wrath, like a person with a fever taking hot medicine.
If a person who is angry practices the mind of loving-kindness, By practicing loving-kindness, anger is not abandoned, yet it is extinguished;
Because practicing the Dharma in this way brings about such correspondence, It is like a person with a feverish illness taking cold medicine.
If one has much ignorance and a dark, shallow mind, practicing both impure conduct and the practice of compassion is of no benefit,
as it only increases delusion— like a person with a wind disorder taking flour-based medicine.
When the human mind, shrouded in delusion and darkness, contemplates causes and conditions, and discerns them with clear observation, that deluded mind is extinguished;
for when the practice of the Dharma accords with this, it is like a person suffering from wind-disease who takes oily medicine.
For example, when a goldsmith fans the charcoal, if he exerts effort at the wrong time, he loses the method of smelting;
if he fans too hastily without knowing the proper time, he may either douse it with water or abandon the process altogether.
If one forces the melting too quickly, it will be ruined; if one stops before it has melted, it will not be refined.
If gold is doused with water at the wrong time, it will rust; if it is left unattended at the wrong time, it will not mature.
One should observe the methods for practicing the Path: exerting effort, gathering the mind, and relinquishing;
for at an improper time, skillful means lose their benefit, and what is not the benefit of the Dharma becomes a non-benefit.
Just as a physician eliminates the three types of ailments— cold, heat, and wind—
so too does the Buddha administer medicine according to the disease,
extinguishing the maladies of lust, anger, and ignorance with their respective remedies.
